"If we have to turn and run--and even if half of us die--it will make no difference to Absalom's troops; they will be looking only for you. You are worth ten thousand of us, and it is better that you stay here in the city and send us help if we need it."
18.4: "If you think that's the best plan, I'll do it," the king finally agreed. So he stood at the gate of the city as all the divisions of troops passed by.
18.5: And the king gave this command to Joab, Abishai, and Ittai: "For my sake, deal gently with young Absalom." And all the troops heard the king give this order to his commanders.
18.6: So the battle began in the forest of Ephraim,
18.7: and the Israelite troops were beaten back by David's men. There was a great slaughter, and twenty thousand men laid down their lives that day.
18.8: The battle raged all across the countryside, and more men died because of the forest than were killed by the sword.
18.9: During the battle, Absalom came unexpectedly upon some of David's men. He tried to escape on his mule, but as he rode beneath the thick branches of a great oak, his head got caught. His mule kept going and left him dangling in the air.
18.10: One of David's men saw what had happened and told Joab, "I saw Absalom dangling in a tree."
18.11: "What?" Joab demanded. "You saw him there and didn't kill him? I would have rewarded you with ten pieces of silver and a hero's belt!"
18.12: "I wouldn't do it for a thousand pieces of silver, "the man replied. "We all heard the king say to you and Abishai and Ittai, `For my sake, please don't harm young Absalom.'
18.13: And if I had betrayed the king by killing his son--and the king would certainly find out who did it--you yourself would be the first to abandon me."
18.14: "Enough of this nonsense," Joab said. Then he took three daggers and plunged them into Absalom's heart as he dangled from the oak still alive.
18.15: Ten of Joab's young armor bearers then surrounded Absalom and killed him.
18.16: Then Joab blew the trumpet, and his men returned from chasing the army of Israel.
18.17: They threw Absalom's body into a deep pit in the forest and piled a great heap of stones over it. And the army of Israel fled to their homes.
18.18: During his lifetime, Absalom had built a monument to himself in the King's Valley, for he had said, "I have no son to carry on my name." He named the monument after himself, and it is known as Absalom's Monument to this day.
18.19: Then Zadok's son Ahimaaz said, "Let me run to the king with the good news that the LORD has saved him from his enemy Absalom."
18.20: "No," Joab told him, "it wouldn't be good news to the king that his son is dead. You can be my messenger some other time, but not today."
18.21: Then Joab said to a man from Cush, "Go tell the king what you have seen." The man bowed and ran off.
18.22: But Ahimaaz continued to plead with Joab, "Whatever happens, please let me go, too.Why should you go, my son?" Joab replied. "There will be no reward for you."
18.23: "Yes, but let me go anyway," he begged. Joab finally said, "All right, go ahead." Then Ahimaaz took a shortcut across the plain of the Jordan and got to Mahanaim ahead of the man from Cush.
18.24: While David was sitting at the city gate, the watchman climbed to the roof of the gateway by the wall. As he looked, he saw a lone man running toward them.
18.25: He shouted the news down to David, and the king replied, "If he is alone, he has news." As the messenger came closer,
18.26: the watchman saw another man running toward them. He shouted down, "Here comes another one!" The king replied, "He also will have news."
18.27: "The first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok," the watchman said. "He is a good man and comes with good news," the king replied.
18.28: Then Ahimaaz cried out to the king, "All is well!" He bowed low with his face to the ground and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has handed over the rebels who dared to stand against you."
18.29: "What about young Absalom?" the king demanded. "Is he all right?" Ahimaaz replied, "When Joab told me to come, there was a lot of commotion. But I didn't know what was happening."
18.30: "Wait here," the king told him. So Ahimaaz stepped aside.
18.31: Then the man from Cush arrived and said, "I have good news for my lord the king. Today the LORD has rescued you from all those who rebelled against you."
18.32: "What about young Absalom?" the king demanded. "Is he all right?" And the Cushite replied, "May all of your enemies, both now and in the future, be as that young man is!"
18.33: The king was overcome with emotion. He went up to his room over the gateway and burst into tears. And as he went, he cried, "O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I could have died instead of you! O Absalom, my son, my son."

19.1: Word soon reached Joab that the king was weeping and mourning for Absalom.
19.2: As the troops heard of the king's deep grief for his son, the joy of that day's victory was turned into deep sadness.
19.3: They crept back into the city as though they were ashamed and had been beaten in battle.
19.4: The king covered his face with his hands and kept on weeping, "O my son Absalom! O Absalom, my son, my son!"
19.5: Then Joab went to the king's room and said to him, "We saved your life today and the lives of your sons, your daughters, and your wives and concubines. Yet you act like this, making us feel ashamed, as though we had done something wrong.
19.6: You seem to love those who hate you and hate those who love you. You have made it clear today that we mean nothing to you. If Absalom had lived and all of us had died, you would be pleased.
19.7: Now go out there and congratulate the troops, for I swear by the LORD that if you don't, not a single one of them will remain here tonight. Then you will be worse off than you have ever been."
19.8: So the king went out and sat at the city gate, and as the news spread throughout the city that he was there, everyone went to him. Meanwhile, the Israelites who supported Absalom had fled to their homes.
19.9: And throughout the tribes of Israel there was much discussion and argument going on. The people were saying, "The king saved us from our enemies, the Philistines, but Absalom chased him out of the country.
19.10: Now Absalom, whom we anointed to rule over us, is dead. Let's ask David to come back and be our king again."
19.11: Then King David sent Zadok and Abiathar, the priests, to say to the leaders of Judah, "Why are you the last ones to reinstate the king? For I have heard that all Israel is ready, and only you are holding out.
19.12: Yet you are my relatives, my own tribe, my own flesh and blood! Why are you the last ones to welcome me back?"
19.13: And David told them to tell Amasa, "Since you are my nephew, may God strike me dead if I do not appoint you as commander of my army in place of Joab."
19.14: Then Amasa convinced all the leaders of Judah, and they responded unanimously. They sent word to the king, "Return to us, and bring back all those who are with you."
19.15: So the king started back to Jerusalem. And when he arrived at the Jordan River, the people of Judah came to Gilgal to meet him and escort him across the river.
19.16: Then Shimei son of Gera, the man from Bahurim in Benjamin, hurried across with the men of Judah to welcome King David.
19.17: A thousand men from the tribe of Benjamin were with him, including Ziba, the servant of Saul, and Ziba's fifteen sons and twenty servants. They rushed down to the Jordan to arrive ahead of the king.
19.18: They all crossed the ford and worked hard ferrying the king's household across the river, helping them in every way they could. As the king was about to cross the river, Shimei fell down before him.
19.19: "My lord the king, please forgive me," he pleaded. "Forget the terrible thing I did when you left Jerusalem.
19.20: I know how much I sinned. That is why I have come here today, the very first person in all Israel to greet you."
19.21: Then Abishai son of Zeruiah said, "Shimei should die, for he cursed the LORD's anointed king!"
19.22: "What am I going to do with you sons of Zeruiah!" David exclaimed. "This is not a day for execution but for celebration! I am once again the king of Israel!"
19.23: Then, turning to Shimei, David vowed, "Your life will be spared."
19.24: Now Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, arrived from Jerusalem to meet the king. He had not washed his feet or clothes nor trimmed his beard since the day the king left Jerusalem.
19.25: "Why didn't you come with me, Mephibosheth?" the king asked him.
19.26: Mephibosheth replied, "My lord the king, my servant Ziba deceived me. I told him, `Saddle my donkey so that I can go with the king.' For as you know I am crippled.
19.27: Ziba has slandered me by saying that I refused to come. But I know that you are like an angel of God, so do what you think is best.
19.28: All my relatives and I could expect only death from you, my lord, but instead you have honored me among those who eat at your own table! So how can I complain?"
19.29: "All right," David replied. "My decision is that you and Ziba will divide your land equally between you."
19.30: "Give him all of it," Mephibosheth said. "I am content just to have you back again, my lord!"
19.31: Barzillai of Gilead now arrived from Rogelim to conduct the king across the Jordan.
19.32: He was very old, about eighty, and very wealthy. He was the one who had provided food for the king during his stay in Mahanaim.
19.33: "Come across with me and live in Jerusalem," the king said to Barzillai. "I will take care of you there."
19.34: "No," he replied, "I am far too old for that.
19.35: I am eighty years old today, and I can no longer enjoy anything. Food and wine are no longer tasty, and I cannot hear the musicians as they play. I would only be a burden to my lord the king.
19.36: Just to go across the river with you is all the honor I need!
19.37: Then let me return again to die in my own town, where my father and mother are buried. But here is my son Kimham. Let him go with you and receive whatever good things you want to give him."
19.38: "Good," the king agreed. "Kimham will go with me, and I will do for him whatever I would have done for you."
19.39: So all the people crossed the Jordan with the king. After David had blessed and embraced him, Barzillai returned to his own home.
19.40: The king then went on to Gilgal, taking Kimham with him. All the army of Judah and half the army of Israel escorted him across the river.
19.41: But the men of Israel complained to the king that the men of Judah had gotten to do most of the work in helping him cross the Jordan.
19.42: "Why not?" the men of Judah replied. "The king is one of our own tribe. Why should this make you angry? We have charged him nothing. And he hasn't fed us or even given us gifts!"
19.43: "But there are ten tribes in Israel," the others replied. "So we have ten times as much right to the king as you do. Why did you treat us with such contempt? Remember, we were the first to speak of bringing him back to be our king again." The argument continued back and forth, and the men of Judah were very harsh in their replies.

20.1: Then a troublemaker named Sheba son of Bicri, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, blew a trumpet and shouted, "We have nothing to do with David. We want no part of this son of Jesse. Come on, you men of Israel, let's all go home!"
20.2: So the men of Israel deserted David and followed Sheba. But the men of Judah stayed with their king and escorted him from the Jordan River to Jerusalem.
20.3: When the king arrived at his palace in Jerusalem, he instructed that the ten concubines he had left to keep house should be placed in seclusion. Their needs were to be cared for, he said, but he would no longer sleep with them. So each of them lived like a widow until she died.
20.4: Then the king instructed Amasa to mobilize the army of Judah within three days and to report back at that time.
20.5: So Amasa went out to notify the troops, but it took him longer than the three days he had been given.
20.6: Then David said to Abishai, "That troublemaker Sheba is going to hurt us more than Absalom did. Quick, take my troops and chase after him before he gets into a fortified city where we can't reach him."
20.7: So Abishai and Joab set out after Sheba with an elite guard from Joab's army and the king's own bodyguard.
20.8: As they arrived at the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa met them, coming from the opposite direction. Joab was wearing his uniform with a dagger strapped to his belt. As he stepped forward to greet Amasa, he secretly slipped the dagger from its sheath.
20.9: "How are you, my cousin?" Joab said and took him by the beard with his right hand as though to kiss him.
20.10: Amasa didn't notice the dagger in his left hand, and Joab stabbed him in the stomach with it so that his insides gushed out onto the ground. Joab did not need to strike again, and Amasa soon died. Joab and his brother Abishai left him lying there and continued after Sheba.
20.11: One of Joab's young officers shouted to Amasa's troops, "If you are for Joab and David, come and follow Joab."
20.12: But Amasa lay in his blood in the middle of the road, and Joab's officer saw that a crowd was gathering around to stare at him. So he pulled him off the road into a field and threw a cloak over him.
20.13: With Amasa's body out of the way, everyone went on with Joab to capture Sheba.
20.14: Meanwhile, Sheba had traveled across Israel to mobilize his own clan of Bicri at the city of Abel-beth-maacah.
20.15: When Joab's forces arrived, they attacked Abel-beth-maacah and built a ramp against the city wall and began battering it down.
20.16: But a wise woman in the city called out to Joab, "Listen to me, Joab. Come over here so I can talk to you."
20.17: As he approached, the woman asked, "Are you Joab?I am," he replied. So she said, "Listen carefully to your servant.I'm listening," he said.
20.18: Then she continued, "There used to be a saying, `If you want to settle an argument, ask advice at the city of Abel.'
20.19: I am one who is peace loving and faithful in Israel. But you are destroying a loyal city. Why do you want to destroy what belongs to the LORD?"
20.20: And Joab replied, "Believe me, I don't want to destroy your city!
20.21: All I want is a man named Sheba son of Bicri from the hill country of Ephraim, who has revolted against King David. If you hand him over to me, we will leave the city in peace.All right," the woman replied, "we will throw his head over the wall to you."
20.22: Then the woman went to the people with her wise advice, and they cut off Sheba's head and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet and called his troops back from the attack, and they all returned to their homes. Joab returned to the king at Jerusalem.
20.23: Joab once again became the commander of David's army. Benaiah son of Jehoiada was commander of the king's bodyguard.
20.24: Adoniram was in charge of the labor force. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the royal historian.
20.25: Sheva was the court secretary. Zadok and Abiathar were the priests.
20.26: Ira the Jairite was David's personal priest.

21.1: There was a famine during David's reign that lasted for three years, so David asked the LORD about it. And the LORD said, "The famine has come because Saul and his family are guilty of murdering the Gibeonites."
21.2: So King David summoned the Gibeonites. They were not part of Israel but were all that was left of the nation of the Amorites. Israel had sworn not to kill them, but Saul, in his zeal, had tried to wipe them out.
21.3: David asked them, "What can I do for you to make amends? Tell me so that the LORD will bless his people again."
21.4: "Well, money won't do it," the Gibeonites replied. "And we don't want to see the Israelites executed in revenge.What can I do then?" David asked. "Just tell me and I will do it for you."
21.5: Then they replied, "It was Saul who planned to destroy us, to keep us from having any place at all in Israel.
21.6: So let seven of Saul's sons or grandsons be handed over to us, and we will execute them before the LORD at Gibeon, on the mountain of the LORD. All right," the king said, "I will do it."
21.7: David spared Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, who was Saul's grandson, because of the oath David and Jonathan had sworn before the LORD.
21.8: But he gave them Saul's two sons Armoni and Mephibosheth, whose mother was Rizpah daughter of Aiah. He also gave them the five sons of Saul's daughter Merab, the wife of Adriel son of Barzillai from Meholah.
21.9: The men of Gibeon executed them on the mountain before the LORD. So all seven of them died together at the beginning of the barley harvest.
21.10: Then Rizpah, the mother of two of the men, spread sackcloth on a rock and stayed there the entire harvest season. She prevented vultures from tearing at their bodies during the day and stopped wild animals from eating them at night.
21.11: When David learned what Rizpah, Saul's concubine, had done,
21.12: he went to the people of Jabesh-gilead and asked for the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan. (When Saul and Jonathan had died in a battle with the Philistines, it was the people of Jabesh-gilead who had retrieved their bodies from the public square of the Philistine city of Beth-shan.)
21.13: So David brought the bones of Saul and Jonathan, as well as the bones of the men the Gibeonites had executed.
21.14: He buried them all in the tomb of Kish, Saul's father, at the town of Zela in the land of Benjamin. After that, God ended the famine in the land of Israel.
21.15: Once again the Philistines were at war with Israel. And when David and his men were in the thick of battle, David became weak and exhausted.
21.16: Ishbi-benob was a descendant of the giants; his bronze spearhead weighed more than seven pounds, and he was armed with a new sword. He had cornered David and was about to kill him.
21.17: But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his rescue and killed the Philistine. After that, David's men declared, "You are not going out to battle again! Why should we risk snuffing out the light of Israel?"
21.18: After this, there was another battle against the Philistines at Gob. As they fought, Sibbecai from Hushah killed Saph, another descendant of the giants.
21.19: In still another battle at Gob, Elhanan son of Jair from Bethlehem killed the brother of Goliath of Gath. The handle of his spear was as thick as a weaver's beam!
21.20: In another battle with the Philistines at Gath, a huge man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot--a descendant of the giants--
21.21: defied and taunted Israel. But he was killed by Jonathan, the son of David's brother Shimea.
21.22: These four Philistines were descended from the giants of Gath, but they were killed by David and his warriors.

22.1: David sang this song to the LORD after the LORD had rescued him from all his enemies and from Saul.
22.2: These are the words he sang: "The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my savior;
22.3: my God is my rock, in whom I find protection. He is my shield, the strength of my salvation, and my stronghold, my high tower, my savior, the one who saves me from violence.
22.4: I will call on the LORD, who is worthy of praise, for he saves me from my enemies.
22.5: "The waves of death surrounded me; the floods of destruction swept over me.
22.6: The grave wrapped its ropes around me; death itself stared me in the face.
22.7: But in my distress I cried out to the LORD; yes, I called to my God for help. He heard me from his sanctuary; my cry reached his ears.
22.8: "Then the earth quaked and trembled; the foundations of the heavens shook; they quaked because of his anger.
22.9: Smoke poured from his nostrils; fierce flames leaped from his mouth; glowing coals flamed forth from him.
22.10: He opened the heavens and came down; dark storm clouds were beneath his feet.
22.11: Mounted on a mighty angel, he flew, soaring on the wings of the wind.
22.12: He shrouded himself in darkness, veiling his approach with dense rain clouds.
22.13: A great brightness shone before him, and bolts of lightning blazed forth.
22.14: The LORD thundered from heaven; the Most High gave a mighty shout.
22.15: He shot his arrows and scattered his enemies; his lightning flashed, and they were confused.
22.16: Then at the command of the LORD, at the blast of his breath, the bottom of the sea could be seen, and the foundations of the earth were laid bare.
22.17: "He reached down from heaven and rescued me; he drew me out of deep waters.
22.18: He delivered me from my powerful enemies, from those who hated me and were too strong for me.
22.19: They attacked me at a moment when I was weakest, but the LORD upheld me.
22.20: He led me to a place of safety; he rescued me because he delights in me.
22.21: The LORD rewarded me for doing right; he compensated me because of my innocence.
22.22: For I have kept the ways of the LORD; I have not turned from my God to follow evil.
22.23: For all his laws are constantly before me; I have never abandoned his principles.
22.24: I am blameless before God; I have kept myself from sin.
22.25: The LORD rewarded me for doing right, because of my innocence in his sight.
22.26: "To the faithful you show yourself faithful; to those with integrity you show integrity.
22.27: To the pure you show yourself pure, but to the wicked you show yourself hostile.
22.28: You rescue those who are humble, but your eyes are on the proud to humiliate them.
22.29: O LORD, you are my light; yes, LORD, you light up my darkness.
22.30: In your strength I can crush an army; with my God I can scale any wall.
22.31: "As for God, his way is perfect. All the LORD's promises prove true. He is a shield for all who look to him for protection.
22.32: For who is God except the LORD? Who but our God is a solid rock?
22.33: God is my strong fortress; he has made my way safe.
22.34: He makes me as surefooted as a deer, leading me safely along the mountain heights.
22.35: He prepares me for battle; he strengthens me to draw a bow of bronze.
22.36: You have given me the shield of your salvation; your help has made me great.
22.37: You have made a wide path for my feet to keep them from slipping.
22.38: "I chased my enemies and destroyed them; I did not stop until they were conquered.
22.39: I consumed them; I struck them down so they could not get up; they fell beneath my feet.
22.40: You have armed me with strength for the battle; you have subdued my enemies under my feet.
22.41: You made them turn and run; I have destroyed all who hated me.
22.42: They called for help, but no one came to rescue them. They cried to the LORD, but he refused to answer them.
22.43: I ground them as fine as the dust of the earth; I swept them into the gutter like dirt.
22.44: "You gave me victory over my accusers. You preserved me as the ruler over nations; people I don't even know now serve me.
22.45: Foreigners cringe before me; as soon as they hear of me, they submit.
22.46: They all lose their courage and come trembling from their strongholds.
22.47: "The LORD lives! Blessed be my rock! May God, the rock of my salvation, be exalted!
22.48: He is the God who pays back those who harm me; he subdues the nations under me
22.49: and rescues me from my enemies. You hold me safe beyond the reach of my enemies; you save me from violent opponents.
22.50: For this, O LORD, I will praise you among the nations; I will sing joyfully to your name.
22.51: You give great victories to your king; you show unfailing love to your anointed, to David and all his descendants forever."

23.1: These are the last words of David: "David, the son of Jesse, speaks--David, the man to whom God gave such wonderful success, David, the man anointed by the God of Jacob, David, the sweet psalmist of Israel.
23.2: "The Spirit of the LORD speaks through me; his words are upon my tongue.
23.3: The God of Israel spoke. The Rock of Israel said to me: `The person who rules righteously, who rules in the fear of God,
23.4: he is like the light of the morning, like the sunrise bursting forth in a cloudless sky, like the refreshing rains that bring tender grass from the earth.'
23.5: "It is my family God has chosen! Yes, he has made an everlasting covenant with me. His agreement is eternal, final, sealed. He will constantly look after my safety and success.
23.6: But the godless are like thorns to be thrown away, for they tear the hand that touches them.
23.7: One must be armed to chop them down; they will be utterly consumed with fire."
23.8: These are the names of David's mightiest men. The first was Jashobeam the Hacmonite, who was commander of the Three--the three greatest warriors among David's men. He once used his spear to kill eight hundred enemy warriors in a single battle.
23.9: Next in rank among the Three was Eleazar son of Dodai, a descendant of Ahoah. Once Eleazar and David stood together against the Philistines when the entire Israelite army had fled.
23.10: He killed Philistines until his hand was too tired to lift his sword, and the LORD gave him a great victory that day. The rest of the army did not return until it was time to collect the plunder!
23.11: Next in rank was Shammah son of Agee from Harar. One time the Philistines gathered at Lehi and attacked the Israelites in a field full of lentils. The Israelite army fled,
23.12: but Shammah held his ground in the middle of the field and beat back the Philistines. So the LORD brought about a great victory.
23.13: Once during harvesttime, when David was at the cave of Adullam, the Philistine army was camped in the valley of Rephaim. The Three (who were among the Thirty--an elite group among David's fighting men) went down to meet him there.
23.14: David was staying in the stronghold at the time, and a Philistine detachment had occupied the town of Bethlehem.
23.15: David remarked longingly to his men, "Oh, how I would love some of that good water from the well in Bethlehem, the one by the gate."
23.16: So the Three broke through the Philistine lines, drew some water from the well, and brought it back to David. But he refused to drink it. Instead, he poured it out before the LORD.
23.17: "The LORD forbid that I should drink this!" he exclaimed. "This water is as precious as the blood of these men who risked their lives to bring it to me." So David did not drink it. This is an example of the exploits of the Three.
23.18: Abishai son of Zeruiah, the brother of Joab, was the leader of the Thirty. He once used his spear to kill three hundred enemy warriors in a single battle. It was by such feats that he became as famous as the Three.
23.19: Abishai was the most famous of the Thirty and was their commander, though he was not one of the Three.
23.20: There was also Benaiah son of Jehoiada, a valiant warrior from Kabzeel. He did many heroic deeds, which included killing two of Moab's mightiest warriors. Another time he chased a lion down into a pit. Then, despite the snow and slippery ground, he caught the lion and killed it.
23.21: Another time, armed only with a club, he killed a great Egyptian warrior who was armed with a spear. Benaiah wrenched the spear from the Egyptian's hand and killed him with it.
23.22: These are some of the deeds that made Benaiah almost as famous as the Three.
23.23: He was more honored than the other members of the Thirty, though he was not one of the Three. And David made him commander of his bodyguard.
23.24: Other members of the Thirty included: Asahel, Joab's brother; Elhanan son of Dodo from Bethlehem;
23.25: Shammah from Harod; Elika from Harod;
23.26: Helez from Pelon; Ira son of Ikkesh from Tekoa;
23.27: Abiezer from Anathoth; Sibbecai from Hushah;
23.28: Zalmon from Ahoah; Maharai from Netophah;
23.29: Heled son of Baanah from Netophah; Ithai son of Ribai from Gibeah (from the tribe of Benjamin);
23.30: Benaiah from Pirathon; Hurai from Nahale-gaash;
23.31: Abi-albon the Arbathite; Azmaveth from Bahurim;
23.32: Eliahba from Shaalbon; the sons of Jashen;
23.33: Jonathan son of Shagee from Harar; Ahiam son of Sharar from Harar;
23.34: Eliphelet son of Ahasbai from Maacah; Eliam son of Ahithophel from Giloh;
23.35: Hezro from Carmel; Paarai from Arba;
23.36: Igal son of Nathan from Zobah; Bani from Gad;
23.37: Zelek from Ammon; Naharai from Beeroth (Joab's armor bearer);
23.38: Ira from Jattir; Gareb from Jattir;
23.39: Uriah the Hittite. There were thirty-seven in all.

24.1: Once again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and he caused David to harm them by taking a census. "Go and count the people of Israel and Judah," the LORD told him.
24.2: So the king said to Joab, the commander of his army, "Take a census of all the people in the land--from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south--so that I may know how many people there are."
24.3: But Joab replied to the king, "May the LORD your God let you live until there are a hundred times as many people in your kingdom as there are now! But why do you want to do this?"
24.4: But the king insisted that they take the census, so Joab and his officers went out to count the people of Israel.
24.5: First they crossed the Jordan and camped at Aroer, south of the town in the valley, in the direction of Gad. Then they went on to Jazer,
24.6: then to Gilead in the land of Tahtim-hodshi and to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon.
24.7: Then they came to the stronghold of Tyre, and all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites. Finally, they went south to Judah as far as Beersheba.
24.8: Having gone through the entire land, they completed their task in nine months and twenty days and then returned to Jerusalem.
24.9: Joab reported the number of people to the king. There were 800,000 men of military age in Israel and 500,000 in Judah.
24.10: But after he had taken the census, David's conscience began to bother him. And he said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly and shouldn't have taken the census. Please forgive me, LORD, for doing this foolish thing."
24.11: The next morning the word of the LORD came to the prophet Gad, who was David's seer. This was the message:
24.12: "Go and say to David, `This is what the LORD says: I will give you three choices. Choose one of these punishments, and I will do it.'"
24.13: So Gad came to David and asked him, "Will you choose three years of famine throughout the land, three months of fleeing from your enemies, or three days of severe plague throughout your land? Think this over and let me know what answer to give the LORD."
24.14: "This is a desperate situation!" David replied to Gad. "But let us fall into the hands of the LORD, for his mercy is great. Do not let me fall into human hands."
24.15: So the LORD sent a plague upon Israel that morning, and it lasted for three days. Seventy thousand people died throughout the nation.
24.16: But as the death angel was preparing to destroy Jerusalem, the LORD relented and said to the angel, "Stop! That is enough!" At that moment the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.
24.17: When David saw the angel, he said to the LORD, "I am the one who has sinned and done wrong! But these people are innocent--what have they done? Let your anger fall against me and my family."
24.18: That day Gad came to David and said to him, "Go and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."
24.19: So David went to do what the LORD had commanded him.
24.20: When Araunah saw the king and his men coming toward him, he came forward and bowed before the king with his face to the ground.
24.21: "Why have you come, my lord?" Araunah asked. And David replied, "I have come to buy your threshing floor and to build an altar to the LORD there, so that the LORD will stop the plague."
24.22: "Take it, my lord, and use it as you wish," Araunah said to David. "Here are oxen for the burnt offering, and you can use the threshing tools and ox yokes for wood to build a fire on the altar.
24.23: I will give it all to you, and may the LORD your God accept your sacrifice."
24.24: But the king replied to Araunah, "No, I insist on buying it, for I cannot present burnt offerings to the LORD my God that have cost me nothing." So David paid him fifty pieces of silver for the threshing floor and the oxen.
24.25: David built an altar there to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. And the LORD answered his prayer, and the plague was stopped.

1.1: Now King David was very old, and no matter how many blankets covered him, he could not keep warm.
1.2: So his advisers told him, "We will find a young virgin who will wait on you and be your nurse. She will lie in your arms and keep you warm."
1.3: So they searched throughout the country for a beautiful girl, and they found Abishag from Shunem and brought her to the king.
1.4: The girl was very beautiful, and she waited on the king and took care of him. But the king had no sexual relations with her.
1.5: About that time David's son Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith, decided to make himself king in place of his aged father. So he provided himself with chariots and horses and recruited fifty men to run in front of him.
1.6: Now his father, King David, had never disciplined him at any time, even by asking, "What are you doing?" Adonijah was a very handsome man and had been born next after Absalom.
1.7: Adonijah took Joab son of Zeruiah and Abiathar the priest into his confidence, and they agreed to help him become king.
1.8: But among those who remained loyal to David and refused to support Adonijah were Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David's personal bodyguard.
1.9: Adonijah went to the stone of Zoheleth near the spring of En-rogel, where he sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened calves. He invited all his brothers--the other sons of King David--and all the royal officials of Judah.
1.10: But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, or Benaiah, or the king's bodyguard, or his brother Solomon.
1.11: Then Nathan the prophet went to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, and asked her, "Did you realize that Haggith's son, Adonijah, has made himself king and that our lord David doesn't even know about it?
1.12: If you want to save your own life and the life of your son Solomon, follow my counsel.
1.13: Go at once to King David and say to him, `My lord, didn't you promise me that my son Solomon would be the next king and would sit upon your throne? Then why has Adonijah become king?'
1.14: And while you are still talking with him, I will come and confirm everything you have said."
1.15: So Bathsheba went into the king's bedroom. He was very old now, and Abishag was taking care of him.
1.16: Bathsheba bowed low before him. "What can I do for you?" he asked her.
1.17: She replied, "My lord, you vowed to me by the LORD your God that my son Solomon would be the next king and would sit on your throne.
1.18: But instead, Adonijah has become the new king, and you do not even know about it.
1.19: He has sacrificed many oxen, fattened calves, and sheep, and he has invited all your sons and Abiathar the priest and Joab, the commander of the army. But he did not invite your servant Solomon.
1.20: And now, my lord the king, all Israel is waiting for your decision as to who will become king after you.
1.21: If you do not act, my son Solomon and I will be treated as criminals as soon as you are dead."
1.22: While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet arrived.
1.23: The king's advisers told him, "Nathan the prophet is here to see you." Nathan went in and bowed low before the king.
1.24: He asked, "My lord, have you decided that Adonijah will be the next king and that he will sit on your throne?
1.25: Today he has sacrificed many oxen, fattened calves, and sheep, and he has invited your sons to attend the celebration. He also invited Joab, the commander of the army, and Abiathar the priest. They are feasting and drinking with him and shouting, `Long live King Adonijah!'
1.26: But I myself, your servant, was not invited; neither were Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, nor Solomon.
1.27: Has my lord really done this without letting any of his servants know who should be the next king?"
1.28: "Call Bathsheba," David said. So she came back in and stood before the king.
1.29: And the king vowed, "As surely as the LORD lives, who has rescued me from every danger,
1.30: today I decree that your son Solomon will be the next king and will sit on my throne, just as I swore to you before the LORD, the God of Israel."
1.31: Then Bathsheba bowed low before him again and exclaimed, "May my lord King David live forever!"
1.32: Then King David ordered, "Call Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada." When they came into the king's presence,
1.33: the king said to them, "Take Solomon and my officers down to Gihon Spring. Solomon is to ride on my personal mule.
1.34: There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet are to anoint him king over Israel. Then blow the trumpets and shout, `Long live King Solomon!'
1.35: When you bring him back here, he will sit on my throne. He will succeed me as king, for I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and Judah."
1.36: "Amen!" Benaiah son of Jehoiada replied. "May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, decree it to be so.
1.37: And may the LORD be with Solomon as he has been with you, and may he make Solomon's reign even greater than yours!"
1.38: So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the king's bodyguard took Solomon down to Gihon Spring, and Solomon rode on King David's personal mule.
1.39: There Zadok the priest took a flask of olive oil from the sacred tent and poured it on Solomon's head. Then the trumpets were blown, and all the people shouted, "Long live King Solomon!"
1.40: And all the people returned with Solomon to Jerusalem, playing flutes and shouting for joy. The celebration was so joyous and noisy that the earth shook with the sound.
1.41: Adonijah and his guests heard the celebrating and shouting just as they were finishing their banquet. When Joab heard the sound of trumpets, he asked, "What's going on? Why is the city in such an uproar?"
1.42: And while he was still speaking, Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest arrived. "Come in," Adonijah said to him, "for you are a good man. You must have good news."
1.43: "Not at all!" Jonathan replied. "Our lord King David has just declared Solomon king!
1.44: The king sent him down to Gihon Spring with Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada, protected by the king's bodyguard. They had him ride on the king's own mule,
1.45: and Zadok and Nathan have anointed him as the new king. They have just returned, and the whole city is celebrating and rejoicing. That's what all the noise is about.
1.46: Moreover, Solomon is now sitting on the royal throne as king.
1.47: All the royal officials went to King David and congratulated him, saying, `May your God make Solomon's fame even greater than your own, and may Solomon's kingdom be even greater than yours!' Then the king bowed his head in worship as he lay in his bed,
1.48: and he spoke these words: `Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who today has chosen someone to sit on my throne while I am still alive to see it.'"
1.49: Then all of Adonijah's guests jumped up in panic from the banquet table and quickly went their separate ways.
1.50: Adonijah himself was afraid of Solomon, so he rushed to the sacred tent and caught hold of the horns of the altar.
1.51: Word soon reached Solomon that Adonijah had seized the horns of the altar and that he was pleading, "Let Solomon swear today that he will not kill me!"
1.52: Solomon replied, "If he proves himself to be loyal, he will not be harmed. But if he does not, he will die."
1.53: So King Solomon summoned Adonijah, and they brought him down from the altar. He came and bowed low before the king, and Solomon dismissed him, saying, "Go on home."

2.1: As the time of King David's death approached, he gave this charge to his son Solomon:
2.2: "I am going where everyone on earth must someday go. Take courage and be a man.
2.3: Observe the requirements of the LORD your God and follow all his ways. Keep each of the laws, commands, regulations, and stipulations written in the law of Moses so that you will be successful in all you do and wherever you go.
2.4: If you do this, then the LORD will keep the promise he made to me: `If your descendants live as they should and follow me faithfully with all their heart and soul, one of them will always sit on the throne of Israel.'
2.5: "And there is something else. You know that Joab son of Zeruiah murdered my two army commanders, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. He pretended that it was an act of war, but it was done in a time of peace, staining his belt and sandals with the blood of war.
2.6: Do with him what you think best, but don't let him die in peace.
2.7: "Be kind to the sons of Barzillai of Gilead. Make them permanent guests of the king, for they took care of me when I fled from your brother Absalom.
2.8: "And remember Shimei son of Gera, the man from Bahurim in Benjamin. He cursed me with a terrible curse as I was fleeing to Mahanaim. When he came down to meet me at the Jordan River, I swore by the LORD that I would not kill him.
2.9: But that oath does not make him innocent. You are a wise man, and you will know how to arrange a bloody death for him."
2.10: Then David died and was buried in the City of David.
2.11: He had reigned over Israel for forty years, seven of them in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem.
2.12: Solomon succeeded him as king, replacing his father, David, and he was firmly established on the throne.
2.13: One day Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith, came to see Bathsheba, Solomon's mother. "Have you come to make trouble?" she asked him. "No," he said, "I come in peace.
2.14: In fact, I have a favor to ask of you.What is it?" she asked.
2.15: He replied, "As you know, the kingdom was mine; everyone expected me to be the next king. But the tables were turned, and everything went to my brother instead; for that is the way the LORD wanted it.
2.16: So now I have just one favor to ask of you. Please don't turn me down.What is it?" she asked.
2.17: He replied, "Speak to King Solomon on my behalf, for I know he will do anything you request. Ask him to give me Abishag, the girl from Shunem, as my wife."
2.18: "All right," Bathsheba replied. "I will speak to the king for you."
2.19: So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak on Adonijah's behalf. The king rose from his throne to meet her, and he bowed down before her. When he sat down on his throne again, he ordered that a throne be brought for his mother, and she sat at his right hand.
2.20: "I have one small request to make of you," she said. "I hope you won't turn me down.What is it, my mother?" he asked. "You know I won't refuse you."
2.21: "Then let your brother Adonijah marry Abishag, the girl from Shunem," she replied.
2.22: "How can you possibly ask me to give Abishag to Adonijah?" Solomon demanded. "You might as well be asking me to give him the kingdom! You know that he is my older brother, and that he has Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah on his side."
2.23: Then King Solomon swore solemnly by the LORD: "May God strike me dead if Adonijah has not sealed his fate with this request.
2.24: The LORD has confirmed me and placed me on the throne of my father, David; he has established my dynasty as he promised. So as surely as the LORD lives, Adonijah will die this very day!"
2.25: So King Solomon ordered Benaiah son of Jehoiada to execute him, and Adonijah was put to death.
2.26: Then the king said to Abiathar the priest, "Go back to your home in Anathoth. You deserve to die, but I will not kill you now, because you carried the Ark of the Sovereign LORD for my father, and you suffered right along with him through all his troubles."
2.27: So Solomon deposed Abiathar from his position as priest of the LORD, thereby fulfilling the decree the LORD had made at Shiloh concerning the descendants of Eli.
2.28: Although he had not followed Absalom earlier, Joab had also joined Adonijah's revolt. When Joab heard about Adonijah's death, he ran to the sacred tent of the LORD and caught hold of the horns of the altar.
2.29: When news of this reached King Solomon, he sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada to execute him.
2.30: Benaiah went into the sacred tent of the LORD and said to Joab, "The king orders you to come out!" But Joab answered, "No, I will die here." So Benaiah returned to the king and told him what Joab had said.
2.31: "Do as he said," the king replied. "Kill him there beside the altar and bury him. This will remove the guilt of his senseless murders from me and from my father's family.
2.32: Then the LORD will repay him for the murders of two men who were more righteous and better than he. For my father was no party to the deaths of Abner son of Ner, commander of the army of Israel, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of the army of Judah.
2.33: May Joab and his descendants be forever guilty of these murders, and may the LORD grant peace to David and his descendants and to his throne forever."
2.34: So Benaiah son of Jehoiada returned to the sacred tent and killed Joab, and Joab was buried at his home in the wilderness.
2.35: Then the king appointed Benaiah to command the army in place of Joab, and he installed Zadok the priest to take the place of Abiathar.
2.36: The king then sent for Shimei and told him, "Build a house here in Jerusalem and live there. But don't step outside the city to go anywhere else.
2.37: On the day you cross the Kidron Valley, you will surely die; your blood will be on your own head."
2.38: Shimei replied, "Your sentence is fair; I will do whatever my lord the king commands." So Shimei lived in Jerusalem for a long time.
2.39: But three years later, two of Shimei's slaves escaped to King Achish of Gath. When Shimei learned where they were,
2.40: he saddled his donkey and went to Gath to search for them. When he had found them, he took them back to Jerusalem.
2.41: Solomon heard that Shimei had left Jerusalem and had gone to Gath and returned.
2.42: So he sent for Shimei and demanded, "Didn't I make you swear by the LORD and warn you not to go anywhere else, or you would surely die? And you replied, `The sentence is fair; I will do as you say.'
2.43: Then why haven't you kept your oath to the LORD and obeyed my command?"
2.44: The king also said to Shimei, "You surely remember all the wicked things you did to my father, King David. May the LORD punish you for them.
2.45: But may I receive the LORD's rich blessings, and may one of David's descendants always sit on this throne."
2.46: Then, at the king's command, Benaiah son of Jehoiada took Shimei outside and killed him. So the kingdom was now firmly in Solomon's grip.

3.1: Solomon made an alliance with Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and married one of his daughters. He brought her to live in the City of David until he could finish building his palace and the Temple of the LORD and the wall around the city.
3.2: At that time the people of Israel sacrificed their offerings at local altars, for a temple honoring the name of the LORD had not yet been built.
3.3: Solomon loved the LORD and followed all the instructions of his father, David, except that Solomon, too, offered sacrifices and burned incense at the local altars.
3.4: The most important of these altars was at Gibeon, so the king went there and sacrificed one thousand burnt offerings.
3.5: That night the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream, and God said, "What do you want? Ask, and I will give it to you!"
3.6: Solomon replied, "You were wonderfully kind to my father, David, because he was honest and true and faithful to you. And you have continued this great kindness to him today by giving him a son to succeed him.
3.7: O LORD my God, now you have made me king instead of my father, David, but I am like a little child who doesn't know his way around.
3.8: And here I am among your own chosen people, a nation so great they are too numerous to count!
3.9: Give me an understanding mind so that I can govern your people well and know the difference between right and wrong. For who by himself is able to govern this great nation of yours?"
3.10: The Lord was pleased with Solomon's reply and was glad that he had asked for wisdom.
3.11: So God replied, "Because you have asked for wisdom in governing my people and have not asked for a long life or riches for yourself or the death of your enemies--
3.12: I will give you what you asked for! I will give you a wise and understanding mind such as no one else has ever had or ever will have!
3.13: And I will also give you what you did not ask for--riches and honor! No other king in all the world will be compared to you for the rest of your life!
3.14: And if you follow me and obey my commands as your father, David, did, I will give you a long life."
3.15: Then Solomon woke up and realized it had been a dream. He returned to Jerusalem and stood before the Ark of the Lord's covenant, where he sacrificed burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then he invited all his officials to a great banquet.
3.16: Some time later, two prostitutes came to the king to have an argument settled.
3.17: "Please, my lord," one of them began, "this woman and I live in the same house. I gave birth to a baby while she was with me in the house.
3.18: Three days later, she also had a baby. We were alone; there were only two of us in the house.
3.19: But her baby died during the night when she rolled over on it.
3.20: Then she got up in the night and took my son from beside me while I was asleep. She laid her dead child in my arms and took mine to sleep beside her.
3.21: And in the morning when I tried to nurse my son, he was dead! But when I looked more closely in the morning light, I saw that it wasn't my son at all."
3.22: Then the other woman interrupted, "It certainly was your son, and the living child is mine.No," the first woman said, "the dead one is yours, and the living one is mine." And so they argued back and forth before the king.
3.23: Then the king said, "Let's get the facts straight. Both of you claim the living child is yours, and each says that the dead child belongs to the other.
3.24: All right, bring me a sword." So a sword was brought to the king.
3.25: Then he said, "Cut the living child in two and give half to each of these women!"
3.26: Then the woman who really was the mother of the living child, and who loved him very much, cried out, "Oh no, my lord! Give her the child--please do not kill him!" But the other woman said, "All right, he will be neither yours nor mine; divide him between us!"
3.27: Then the king said, "Do not kill him, but give the baby to the woman who wants him to live, for she is his mother!"
3.28: Word of the king's decision spread quickly throughout all Israel, and the people were awed as they realized the great wisdom God had given him to render decisions with justice.

4.1: So Solomon was king over all Israel,
4.2: and these were his high officials: Azariah son of Zadok was the priest.
4.3: Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha, were court secretaries. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the royal historian.
4.4: Benaiah son of Jehoiada was commander of the army. Zadok and Abiathar were the priests.
4.5: Azariah son of Nathan presided over the district governors. Zabud son of Nathan, a priest, was a trusted adviser to the king.
4.6: Ahishar was manager of palace affairs. Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the labor force.
4.7: Solomon also had twelve district governors who were over all Israel. They were responsible for providing food from the people for the king's household. Each of them arranged provisions for one month of the year.
4.8: These are the names of the twelve governors: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim.
4.9: Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-bethhanan.
4.10: Ben-hesed, in Arubboth, including Socoh and all the land of Hepher.
4.11: Ben-abinadab, in Naphoth-dor. (He was married to Taphath, one of Solomon's daughters.)
4.12: Baana son of Ahilud, in Taanach and Megiddo, all of Beth-shan near Zarethan below Jezreel, and all the territory from Beth-shan to Abel-meholah and over to Jokmeam.
4.13: Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead, including the Towns of Jair (named for Jair son of Manasseh) in Gilead, and in the Argob region of Bashan, including sixty great fortified cities with gates barred with bronze.
4.14: Ahinadab son of Iddo, in Mahanaim.
4.15: Ahimaaz, in Naphtali. (He was married to Basemath, another of Solomon's daughters.)
4.16: Baana son of Hushai, in Asher and in Aloth.
4.17: Jehoshaphat son of Paruah, in Issachar.
4.18: Shimei son of Ela, in Benjamin.
4.19: Geber son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, including the territories of King Sihon of the Amorites and King Og of Bashan. And there was one governor over the land of Judah.
4.20: The people of Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They were very contented, with plenty to eat and drink.
4.21: King Solomon ruled all the kingdoms from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines, as far south as the border of Egypt. The conquered peoples of those lands sent tribute money to Solomon and continued to serve him throughout his lifetime.
4.22: The daily food requirements for Solomon's palace were 150 bushels of choice flour and 300 bushels of meal,
4.23: ten oxen from the fattening pens, twenty pasture-fed cattle, one hundred sheep or goats, as well as deer, gazelles, roebucks, and choice fowl.
4.24: Solomon's dominion extended over all the kingdoms west of the Euphrates River, from Tiphsah to Gaza. And there was peace throughout the entire land.
4.25: Throughout the lifetime of Solomon, all of Judah and Israel lived in peace and safety. And from Dan to Beersheba, each family had its own home and garden.
4.26: Solomon had four thousand stalls for his chariot horses and twelve thousand horses.
4.27: The district governors faithfully provided food for King Solomon and his court, each during his assigned month.
4.28: They also brought the necessary barley and straw for the royal horses in the stables.
4.29: God gave Solomon great wisdom and understanding, and knowledge too vast to be measured.
4.30: In fact, his wisdom exceeded that of all the wise men of the East and the wise men of Egypt.
4.31: He was wiser than anyone else, including Ethan the Ezrahite and Heman, Calcol, and Darda--the sons of Mahol. His fame spread throughout all the surrounding nations.
4.32: He composed some 3,000 proverbs and wrote 1,005 songs.
4.33: He could speak with authority about all kinds of plants, from the great cedar of Lebanon to the tiny hyssop that grows from cracks in a wall. He could also speak about animals, birds, reptiles, and fish.
4.34: And kings from every nation sent their ambassadors to listen to the wisdom of Solomon.

5.1: King Hiram of Tyre had always been a loyal friend of David, so when he learned that David's son Solomon was the new king of Israel, Hiram sent ambassadors to congratulate him.
5.2: Then Solomon sent this message back to Hiram:
5.3: "You know that my father, David, was not able to build a Temple to honor the name of the LORD his God because of the many wars he waged with surrounding nations. He could not build until the LORD gave him victory over all his enemies.
5.4: But now the LORD my God has given me peace on every side, and I have no enemies and all is well.
5.5: So I am planning to build a Temple to honor the name of the LORD my God, just as he instructed my father that I should do. For the LORD told him, `Your son, whom I will place on your throne, will build the Temple to honor my name.'
5.6: Now please command that cedars from Lebanon be cut for me. Let my men work alongside yours, and I will pay your men whatever wages you ask. As you know, there is no one among us who can cut timber like you Sidonians!"
5.7: When Hiram received Solomon's message, he was very pleased and said, "Praise the LORD for giving David a wise son to be king of the great nation of Israel."
5.8: Then he sent this reply to Solomon: "I have received your message, and I will do as you have asked concerning the timber. I can supply you with both cedar and cypress.
5.9: My servants will bring the logs from the Lebanon mountains to the Mediterranean Sea and build them into rafts. We will float them along the coast to whatever place you choose. Then we will break the rafts apart and deliver the timber to you. You can pay me with food for my household."
5.10: So Hiram produced for Solomon as much cedar and cypress timber as he desired.
5.11: In return Solomon sent him an annual payment of 100,000 bushels of wheat for his household and 110,000 gallons of olive oil.
5.12: So the LORD gave great wisdom to Solomon just as he had promised. And Hiram and Solomon made a formal alliance of peace.
5.13: Then King Solomon enlisted 30,000 laborers from all Israel.
5.14: He sent them to Lebanon in shifts, 10,000 every month, so that each man would be one month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of this labor force.
5.15: Solomon also enlisted 70,000 common laborers, 80,000 stonecutters in the hill country,
5.16: and 3,600 foremen to supervise the work.
5.17: At the king's command, the stonecutters quarried and shaped costly blocks of stone for the foundation of the Temple.
5.18: Men from the city of Gebal helped Solomon's and Hiram's builders prepare the timber and stone for the Temple.

6.1: It was in midspring, during the fourth year of Solomon's reign, that he began the construction of the Temple of the LORD. This was 480 years after the people of Israel were delivered from their slavery in the land of Egypt.
6.2: The Temple that King Solomon built for the LORD was 90 feet long, 30 feet wide, and 45 feet high.
6.3: The foyer at the front of the Temple was 30 feet wide, running across the entire width of the Temple. It projected outward 15 feet from the front of the Temple.
6.4: Solomon also made narrow, recessed windows throughout the Temple.
6.5: A complex of rooms was built against the outer walls of the Temple, all the way around the sides and rear of the building.
6.6: The complex was three stories high, the bottom floor being 7 1/2 feet wide, the second floor 9 feet wide, and the top floor 10 1/2 feet wide. The rooms were connected to the walls of the Temple by beams resting on ledges built out from the wall. So the beams were not inserted into the walls themselves.
6.7: The stones used in the construction of the Temple were prefinished at the quarry, so the entire structure was built without the sound of hammer, ax, or any other iron tool at the building site.
6.8: The entrance to the bottom floor was on the south side of the Temple. There were winding stairs going up to the second floor, and another flight of stairs between the second and third floors.
6.9: After completing the Temple structure, Solomon put in a ceiling made of beams and planks of cedar.
6.10: As already stated, there was a complex of rooms on three sides of the building, attached to the Temple walls by cedar timbers. Each story of the complex was 7 1/2 feet high.
6.11: Then the LORD gave this message to Solomon:
6.12: "Concerning this Temple you are building, if you keep all my laws and regulations and obey all my commands, I will fulfill through you the promise I made to your father, David.
6.13: I will live among the people of Israel and never forsake my people."
6.14: So Solomon finished building the Temple.
6.15: The entire inside, from floor to ceiling, was paneled with wood. He paneled the walls and ceilings with cedar, and he used cypress for the floors.
6.16: He partitioned off an inner sanctuary--the Most Holy Place--at the far end of the Temple. It was 30 feet deep and was paneled with cedar from floor to ceiling.
6.17: The main room of the Temple, outside the Most Holy Place, was 60 feet long.
6.18: Cedar paneling completely covered the stone walls throughout the Temple, and the paneling was decorated with carvings of gourds and open flowers.
6.19: Solomon prepared the inner sanctuary in the rear of the Temple, where the Ark of the LORD's covenant would be placed.
6.20: This inner sanctuary was 30 feet long, 30 feet wide, and 30 feet high. Solomon overlaid its walls and ceiling with pure gold. He also overlaid the altar made of cedar.
6.21: Then he overlaid the rest of the Temple's interior with pure gold, and he made gold chains to protect the entrance to the Most Holy Place.
6.22: So he finished overlaying the entire Temple with gold, including the altar that belonged to the Most Holy Place.
6.23: Within the inner sanctuary Solomon placed two cherubim made of olive wood, each 15 feet tall.
6.24: The wingspan of each of the cherubim was 15 feet, each wing being 7 1/2 feet long.
6.25: The two cherubim were identical in shape and size;
6.27: Solomon placed them side by side in the inner sanctuary of the Temple. Their outspread wings reached from wall to wall, while their inner wings touched at the center of the room.
6.28: He overlaid the two cherubim with gold.
6.29: All the walls of the inner sanctuary and the main room were decorated with carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers.
6.30: The floor in both rooms was overlaid with gold.
6.31: For the entrance to the inner sanctuary, Solomon made double doors of olive wood with five-sided doorposts.
6.32: These doors were decorated with carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and the doors were overlaid with gold.
6.33: Then he made four-sided doorposts of olive wood for the entrance to the Temple.
6.34: There were two folding doors of cypress wood, and each door was hinged to fold back upon itself.
6.35: These doors were decorated with carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and the doors were overlaid with gold.
6.36: The walls of the inner courtyard were built so that there was one layer of cedar beams after every three layers of hewn stone.
6.37: The foundation of the LORD's Temple was laid in midspring of the fourth year of Solomon's reign.
6.38: The entire building was completed in every detail by midautumn of the eleventh year of his reign. So it took seven years to build the Temple.

7.1: Solomon also built a palace for himself, and it took him thirteen years to complete the construction.
7.2: One of Solomon's buildings was called the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon. It was 150 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high. The great cedar ceiling beams rested on four rows of cedar pillars.
7.3: It had a cedar roof supported by forty-five rafters that rested on three rows of pillars, fifteen in each row.
7.4: On each of the side walls there were three rows of windows facing each other.
7.5: All the doorways were rectangular in frame; they were in sets of three, facing each other.
7.6: He also built the Hall of Pillars, which was 75 feet long and 45 feet wide. There was a porch at its front, covered by a canopy that was supported by pillars.
7.7: There was also the Hall of the Throne, also known as the Hall of Judgment, where Solomon sat to hear legal matters. It was paneled with cedar from floor to ceiling.
7.8: Solomon's living quarters surrounded a courtyard behind this hall; they were built the same way. He also built similar living quarters for Pharaoh's daughter, one of his wives.
7.9: All these buildings were built entirely from huge, costly blocks of stone, cut and trimmed to exact measure on all sides.
7.10: Some of the huge foundation stones were 15 feet long, and some were 12 feet long.
7.11: The costly blocks of stone used in the walls were also cut to measure, and cedar beams were also used.
7.12: The walls of the great courtyard were built so that there was one layer of cedar beams after every three layers of hewn stone, just like the walls of the inner courtyard of the LORD's Temple with its entrance foyer.
7.13: King Solomon then asked for a man named Huram to come from Tyre,
7.14: for he was a craftsman skilled in bronze work. He was half Israelite, since his mother was a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father had been a foundry worker from Tyre. So he came to work for King Solomon.
7.15: Huram cast two bronze pillars, each 27 feet tall and 18 feet in circumference.
7.16: For the tops of the pillars he made capitals of molded bronze, each 7 1/2 feet tall.
7.17: Each capital was decorated with seven sets of latticework and interwoven chains.
7.18: He also made two rows of pomegranates that encircled the latticework to decorate the capitals over the pillars.
7.19: The capitals on the columns inside the foyer were shaped like lilies, and they were 6 feet tall.
7.20: Each capital on the two pillars had two hundred pomegranates in two rows around them, beside the rounded surface next to the latticework.
7.21: Huram set the pillars at the entrance of the Temple, one toward the south and one toward the north. He named the one on the south Jakin, and the one on the north Boaz.
7.22: The capitals on the pillars were shaped like lilies. And so the work on the pillars was finished.
7.23: Then Huram cast a large round tank, 15 feet across from rim to rim; it was called the Sea. It was 7 1/2 feet deep and about 45 feet in circumference.
7.24: The Sea was encircled just below its rim by two rows of decorative gourds. There were about six gourds per foot all the way around, and they had been cast as part of the tank.
7.25: The Sea rested on a base of twelve bronze oxen, all facing outward. Three faced north, three faced west, three faced south, and three faced east.
7.26: The walls of the Sea were about three inches thick, and its rim flared out like a cup and resembled a lily blossom. It could hold about 11,000 gallons of water.
7.27: Huram also made ten bronze water carts, each 6 feet long, 6 feet wide, and 4 1/2 feet tall.
7.28: They were constructed with side panels braced with crossbars.
7.29: Both the panels and the crossbars were decorated with carved lions, oxen, and cherubim. Above and below the lions and oxen were wreath decorations.
7.30: Each of these carts had four bronze wheels and bronze axles. At each corner of the carts were supporting posts for the bronze basins; these supports were decorated with carvings of wreaths on each side.
7.31: The top of each cart had a circular frame for the basin. It projected 1 1/2 feet above the cart's top like a round pedestal, and its opening was 2 1/4 feet across; it was decorated on the outside with carvings of wreaths. The panels of the carts were square, not round.
7.32: Under the panels were four wheels that were connected to axles that had been cast as one unit with the cart. The wheels were 2 1/4 feet in diameter
7.33: and were similar to chariot wheels. The axles, spokes, rims, and hubs were all cast from molten bronze.
7.34: There were supports at each of the four corners of the carts, and these, too, were cast as one unit with the cart.
7.35: Around the top of each cart there was a rim 9 inches wide. The supports and side panels were cast as one unit with the cart.
7.36: Carvings of cherubim, lions, and palm trees decorated the panels and supports wherever there was room, and there were wreaths all around.
7.37: All ten water carts were the same size and were made alike, for each was cast from the same mold.
7.38: Huram also made ten bronze basins, one for each cart. Each basin was 6 feet across and could hold 220 gallons of water.
7.39: He arranged five water carts on the south side of the Temple and five on the north side. The Sea was placed at the southeast corner of the Temple.
7.40: He also made the necessary pots, shovels, and basins. So at last Huram completed everything King Solomon had assigned him to make for the Temple of the LORD:
7.41: two pillars, two bowl-shaped capitals on top of the pillars, two networks of chains that decorated the capitals,
7.42: four hundred pomegranates that hung from the chains on the capitals (two rows of pomegranates for each of the chain networks that were hung around the capitals on top of the pillars),
7.43: the ten water carts holding the ten basins,
7.44: the Sea and the twelve oxen under it,
7.45: the pots, the shovels, and the basins. All these utensils for the Temple of the LORD that Huram made for Solomon were made of burnished bronze.
7.46: The king had them cast in clay molds in the Jordan Valley between Succoth and Zarethan.
7.47: Solomon did not weigh all the utensils because there were so many; the weight of the bronze could not be measured.
7.48: So Solomon made all the furnishings of the Temple of the LORD: the gold altar, the gold table for the Bread of the Presence,
7.49: the gold lampstands, five on the south and five on the north, in front of the Most Holy Place, the flower decorations, lamps, and tongs, all of gold,
7.50: the cups, lamp snuffers, basins, dishes, and firepans, all of pure gold, the doors for the entrances to the Most Holy Place and the main room of the Temple, with their fronts overlaid with gold.
7.51: So King Solomon finished all his work on the Temple of the LORD. Then Solomon brought all the gifts his father, David, had dedicated--the silver, the gold, and the other utensils--and he stored them in the treasuries of the LORD's Temple.

8.1: Solomon then summoned the leaders of all the tribes and families of Israel to assemble in Jerusalem. They were to bring the Ark of the LORD's covenant from its location in the City of David, also known as Zion, to its new place in the Temple.
8.2: They all assembled before the king at the annual Festival of Shelters in early autumn.
8.3: When all the leaders of Israel arrived, the priests picked up the Ark.
8.4: Then the priests and Levites took the Ark of the LORD, along with the Tabernacle and all its sacred utensils, and carried them up to the Temple.
8.5: King Solomon and the entire community of Israel sacrificed sheep and oxen before the Ark in such numbers that no one could keep count!
8.6: Then the priests carried the Ark of the LORD's covenant into the inner sanctuary of the Temple--the Most Holy Place--and placed it beneath the wings of the cherubim.
8.7: The cherubim spread their wings over the Ark, forming a canopy over the Ark and its carrying poles.
8.8: These poles were so long that their ends could be seen from the front entrance of the Temple's main room--the Holy Place--but not from outside it. They are still there to this day.
8.9: Nothing was in the Ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed there at Mount Sinai, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel as they were leaving the land of Egypt.
8.10: As the priests came out of the inner sanctuary, a cloud filled the Temple of the LORD.
8.11: The priests could not continue their work because the glorious presence of the LORD filled the Temple.
8.12: Then Solomon prayed, "O LORD, you have said that you would live in thick darkness.
8.13: But I have built a glorious Temple for you, where you can live forever!"
8.14: Then the king turned around to the entire community of Israel standing before him and gave this blessing:
8.15: "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has kept the promise he made to my father, David.
8.16: For he told my father, `From the day I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I have never chosen a city among the tribes of Israel as the place where a temple should be built to honor my name. But now I have chosen David to be king over my people.'"
8.17: Then Solomon said, "My father, David, wanted to build this Temple to honor the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
8.18: But the LORD told him, `It is right for you to want to build the Temple to honor my name,
8.19: but you are not the one to do it. One of your sons will build it instead.'
8.20: "And now the LORD has done what he promised, for I have become king in my father's place. I have built this Temple to honor the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
8.21: And I have prepared a place there for the Ark, which contains the covenant that the LORD made with our ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt."
8.22: Then Solomon stood with his hands lifted toward heaven before the altar of the LORD in front of the entire community of Israel.
8.23: He prayed, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you in all of heaven or earth. You keep your promises and show unfailing love to all who obey you and are eager to do your will.
8.24: You have kept your promise to your servant David, my father. You made that promise with your own mouth, and today you have fulfilled it with your own hands.
8.25: And now, O LORD, God of Israel, carry out your further promise to your servant David, my father. For you said to him, `If your descendants guard their behavior as you have done, they will always reign over Israel.'
8.26: Now, O God of Israel, fulfill this promise to your servant David, my father.
8.27: "But will God really live on earth? Why, even the highest heavens cannot contain you. How much less this Temple I have built!
8.28: Listen to my prayer and my request, O LORD my God. Hear the cry and the prayer that your servant is making to you today.
8.29: May you watch over this Temple both day and night, this place where you have said you would put your name. May you always hear the prayers I make toward this place.
8.30: May you hear the humble and earnest requests from me and your people Israel when we pray toward this place. Yes, hear us from heaven where you live, and when you hear, forgive.
8.31: "If someone wrongs another person and is required to take an oath of innocence in front of the altar at this Temple,
8.32: then hear from heaven and judge between your servants--the accuser and the accused. Punish the guilty party and acquit the one who is innocent.
8.33: "If your people Israel are defeated by their enemies because they have sinned against you, and if they turn to you and call on your name and pray to you here in this Temple,
8.34: then hear from heaven and forgive their sins and return them to this land you gave their ancestors.
8.35: "If the skies are shut up and there is no rain because your people have sinned against you, and then they pray toward this Temple and confess your name and turn from their sins because you have punished them,
8.36: then hear from heaven and forgive the sins of your servants, your people Israel. Teach them to do what is right, and send rain on your land that you have given to your people as their special possession.
8.37: "If there is a famine in the land, or plagues, or crop disease, or attacks of locusts or caterpillars, or if your people's enemies are in the land besieging their towns--whatever the trouble is--
8.38: and if your people offer a prayer concerning their troubles or sorrow, raising their hands toward this Temple,
8.39: then hear from heaven where you live, and forgive. Give your people whatever they deserve, for you alone know the human heart.
8.40: Then they will fear you and walk in your ways as long as they live in the land you gave to our ancestors.
8.41: "And when foreigners hear of you and come from distant lands to worship your great name--
8.42: for they will hear of you and of your mighty miracles and your power--and when they pray toward this Temple,
8.43: then hear from heaven where you live, and grant what they ask of you. Then all the people of the earth will come to know and fear you, just as your own people Israel do. They, too, will know that this Temple I have built bears your name.
8.44: "If your people go out at your command to fight their enemies, and if they pray to the LORD toward this city that you have chosen and toward this Temple that I have built for your name,
8.45: then hear their prayers from heaven and uphold their cause.
8.46: "If they sin against you--and who has never sinned?--you may become angry with them and let their enemies conquer them and take them captive to a foreign land far or near.
8.47: But in that land of exile, they may turn to you again in repentance and pray, `We have sinned, done evil, and acted wickedly.'
8.48: Then if they turn to you with their whole heart and soul and pray toward the land you gave to their ancestors, toward this city you have chosen, and toward this Temple I have built to honor your name,
8.49: then hear their prayers from heaven where you live. Uphold their cause
8.50: and forgive your people who have sinned against you. Make their captors merciful to them,
8.51: for they are your people--your special possession--whom you brought out of the iron-smelting furnace of Egypt.
8.52: "May your eyes be open to my requests and to the requests of your people Israel. Hear and answer them whenever they cry out to you.
8.53: For when you brought our ancestors out of Egypt, O Sovereign LORD, you told your servant Moses that you had separated Israel from among all the nations of the earth to be your own special possession."
8.54: When Solomon finished making these prayers and requests to the LORD, he stood up in front of the altar of the LORD, where he had been kneeling with his hands raised toward heaven.
8.55: He stood there and shouted this blessing over the entire community of Israel:
8.56: "Praise the LORD who has given rest to his people Israel, just as he promised. Not one word has failed of all the wonderful promises he gave through his servant Moses.
8.57: May the LORD our God be with us as he was with our ancestors; may he never forsake us.
8.58: May he give us the desire to do his will in everything and to obey all the commands, laws, and regulations that he gave our ancestors.
8.59: And may these words that I have prayed in the presence of the LORD be before him constantly, day and night, so that the LORD our God may uphold my cause and the cause of his people Israel, fulfilling our daily needs.
8.60: May people all over the earth know that the LORD is God and that there is no other god.
8.61: And may you, his people, always be faithful to the LORD our God. May you always obey his laws and commands, just as you are doing today."
8.62: Then the king and all Israel with him offered sacrifices to the LORD.
8.63: Solomon sacrificed peace offerings to the LORD numbering 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. And so the king and all Israel dedicated the Temple of the LORD.
8.64: That same day the king dedicated the central area of the courtyard in front of the LORD's Temple. He offered burnt offerings, grain offerings, and the fat of peace offerings there, because the bronze altar in the LORD's presence was too small to handle so many offerings.
8.65: Then Solomon and all Israel celebrated the Festival of Shelters in the presence of the LORD their God. A large crowd had gathered from as far away as Lebo-hamath in the north to the brook of Egypt in the south. The celebration went on for fourteen days in all--seven days for the dedication of the altar and seven days for the Festival of Shelters.
8.66: After the festival was over, Solomon sent the people home. They blessed the king as they went, and they were all joyful and happy because the LORD had been good to his servant David and to his people Israel.

9.1: So Solomon finished building the Temple of the LORD, as well as the royal palace. He completed everything he had planned to do.
9.2: Then the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had done before at Gibeon.
9.3: The LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and your request. I have set apart this Temple you have built so that my name will be honored there forever. I will always watch over it and care for it.
