17.26: It’s horrible to persecute a holy lover of God or to strike an honorable man for his integrity!
17.27: Can you bridle your tongue when your heart is under pressure? That’s how you show that you are wise. An understanding heart keeps you cool, calm, and collected, no matter what you’re facing.
17.28: When even a fool bites his tongue he’s considered wise. So shut your mouth when you are provoked— it will make you look smart.

18.1: An unfriendly person isolates himself and seems to care only about his own issues. For his contempt of sound judgment makes him a recluse.
18.2: Senseless people find no pleasure in acquiring true wisdom, for all they want to do is impress you with what they know.
18.3: An ungodly man is always cloaked with disgrace, as dishonor and shame are his companions.
18.4: Words of wisdom are like a fresh, flowing brook— like deep waters that spring forth from within, bubbling up inside the one with understanding.
18.5: It is atrocious when judges show favor to the guilty and deprive the innocent of justice.
18.6: A senseless man jumps headfirst into an argument; he’s just asking for a beating for his reckless words.
18.7: A fool has a big mouth that only gets him into trouble, and he’ll pay the price for what he says.
18.8: The words of a gossip merely reveal the wounds of his own soul, and his slander penetrates into the innermost being.
18.9: The one who is too lazy to look for work is the same one who wastes his life away.
18.10: The character of God is a tower of strength, for the lovers of God delight to run into his heart and be exalted on high.
18.11: The rich, in their conceit, imagine that their wealth is enough to protect them. It becomes their confidence in a day of trouble.
18.12: A man’s heart is the proudest when his downfall is nearest, for he won’t see glory until the Lord sees humility.
18.13: Listen before you speak, for to speak before you’ve heard the facts will bring humiliation.
18.14: The will to live sustains you when you’re sick, but depression crushes courage and leaves you unable to cope.
18.15: The spiritually hungry are always ready to learn more, for their hearts are eager to discover new truths.
18.16: Would you like to meet a very important person? Take a generous gift. It will do wonders to gain entrance into his presence.
18.17: There are two sides to every story. The first one to speak sounds true until you hear the other side and they set the record straight.
18.18: A coin toss resolves a dispute and can put an argument to rest between formidable opponents.
18.19: It is easier to conquer a strong city than to win back a friend whom you’ve offended. Their walls go up, making it nearly impossible to win them back.
18.20: Sharing words of wisdom is satisfying to your inner being. It encourages you to know that you’ve changed someone else’s life.
18.21: Your words are so powerful that they will kill or give life, and the talkative person will reap the consequences.
18.22: When a man finds a wife, he has found a treasure! For she is the gift of God to bring him joy and pleasure. But the one who divorces a good woman loses what is good from his house. To choose an adulteress is both stupid and ungodly.
18.23: The poor plead for help from the rich, but all they get in return is a harsh response.
18.24: Some friendships don’t last for long, but there is one loving friend who is joined to your heart closer than any other!

19.1: It’s better to be honest, even if it leads to poverty, than to live as a dishonest fool.
19.2: The best way to live is with revelation-knowledge, for without it, you’ll grow impatient and run right into error.
19.3: There are some people who ruin their own lives and then blame it all on God.
19.4: Being wealthy means having lots of “friends,” but the poor can’t keep the ones they have.
19.5: Perjury won’t go unpunished, and liars will get all that they deserve.
19.6: Everyone wants to be close to the rich and famous, but a generous person has all the friends he wants!
19.7: When a man is poor, even his family has no use for him. How much more will his “friends” avoid him— for though he begs for help, they won’t respond.
19.8: Do yourself a favor and love wisdom. Learn all you can, then watch your life flourish and prosper!
19.9: Tell lies and you’re going to get caught, and the habitual liar is doomed.
19.10: It doesn’t seem right when you see a fool living in the lap of luxury or a prideful servant ruling over princes.
19.11: An understanding person demonstrates patience, for mercy means holding your tongue. When you are insulted, be quick to forgive and forget it, for you are virtuous when you overlook an offense.
19.12: The rage of a king is like the roar of a lion, but his sweet favor is like a gentle, refreshing rain.
19.13: A rebellious son breaks a father’s heart, and a nagging wife can drive you crazy!
19.14: You can inherit houses and land from your parents, but a good wife only comes as a gracious gift from God!
19.15: Go ahead—be lazy and passive. But you’ll go hungry if you live that way.
19.16: Honor God’s holy instructions and life will go well for you. But if you despise his ways and choose your own plans, you will die.
19.17: Every time you give to the poor you make a loan to the Lord. Don’t worry—you’ll be repaid in full for all the good you’ve done.
19.18: Don’t be afraid to discipline your children while they’re still young enough to learn. Don’t indulge your children or be swayed by their protests.
19.19: A hot-tempered man has to pay the price for his anger. If you bail him out once, you’ll do it a dozen times.
19.20: Listen well to wise counsel and be willing to learn from correction so that by the end of your life you’ll be known for your wisdom.
19.21: A person may have many ideas concerning God’s plan for his life, but only the designs of God’s purpose will succeed in the end.
19.22: A man is charming when he displays tender mercies to others. And a lover of God who is poor and promises nothing is better than a rich liar who never keeps his promises.
19.23: When you live a life of abandoned love, surrendered before the awe of God, here’s what you’ll experience: Abundant life. Continual protection. And complete satisfaction!
19.24: There are some people who pretend they’re hurt— deadbeats who won’t even work to feed themselves.
19.25: If you punish the insolent who don’t know any better, they will learn not to mock. But if you correct a wise man, he will grow even wiser.
19.26: Children who mistreat their parents are an embarrassment to their family and a public disgrace.
19.27: So listen, my child. Don’t reject correction or you will certainly wander from the ways of truth.
19.28: A corrupt witness makes a mockery of justice, for the wicked never play by the rules.
19.29: Judgment is waiting for those who mock the truth, and foolish living invites a beating.

20.1: A drunkard is obnoxious, loud, and argumentative; you’re a fool to get intoxicated with strong drink.
20.2: The rage of a king is like the roar of a lion. Do you really want to go and make him angry?
20.3: A person of honor will put an argument to rest. Only the stupid want to pick a fight.
20.4: If you’re too lazy to plant seed, it’s too bad when you have no harvest on which to feed.
20.5: A man of deep understanding will give good advice, drawing it out from the well within.
20.6: Many will tell you they’re your loyal friends, but who can find one who is truly trustworthy?
20.7: The lovers of God will walk in integrity, and their children are fortunate to have godly parents as their examples.
20.8: A righteous king sits on his judgment seat. He scatters evil away from his kingdom by his wise discernment.
20.9: Which one of us can truly say, “I am free from sin in my life, for my heart is clean and pure”?
20.10: Mark it down: God hates it when you demonstrate a double standard— one for “them” and one for “you.”
20.11: All children show what they’re really like by how they act. You can discern their character, whether they are pure or perverse.
20.12: Lovers of God have been given eyes to see and ears to hear from God.
20.13: If you spend all your time sleeping, you’ll grow poor. So wake up, sleepyhead! Don’t sleep on the job. And then there will be plenty of food on your table.
20.14: The buyer says, as he haggles over the price, “That’s junk. It’s worthless!” Then he goes out and brags, “Look at the great bargain I got!”
20.15: You may have an abundance of wealth, piles of gold and jewels, but there is something of far greater worth: speaking revelation-words of knowledge.
20.16: Anyone stupid enough to guarantee a loan for a stranger deserves to have his property held as security.
20.17: What you obtain dishonestly may seem sweet at first, but sooner or later you’ll live to regret it.
20.18: If you solicit good advice, then your plans will succeed. So don’t charge into battle without wisdom, for wars are won by skillful strategy.
20.19: A blabbermouth will reveal your secrets, so stay away from people who can’t keep their mouths shut.
20.20: If you despise your father or mother, your life will flicker out like a lamp, extinguished into the deepest darkness.
20.21: If an inheritance is gained too early in life, it will not be blessed in the end.
20.22: Don’t ever say, “I’m going to get even with them if it’s the last thing I do!” Wrap God’s grace around your heart and he will be the one to vindicate you.
20.23: The Lord hates double standards— that’s hypocrisy at its worst!
20.24: It is the Lord who directs your life, for each step you take is ordained by God to bring you closer to your destiny. So much of your life, then, remains a mystery!
20.25: Be careful in making a rash promise before God, or you may be trapped by your vow and live to regret it.
20.26: A wise king is able to discern corruption and remove wickedness from his kingdom.
20.27: The spirit God breathed into man is like a living lamp, a shining light searching into the innermost chamber of our being.
20.28: Good leadership is built on love and truth, for kindness and integrity are what keep leaders in their position of trust.
20.29: We admire the young for their strength and beauty, but the dignity of the old is their wisdom.
20.30: When you are punished severely, you learn your lesson well— for painful experiences do wonders to change your life.

21.1: It’s as easy for God to steer a king’s heart for his purposes as it is for him to direct the course of a stream.
21.2: We may think we’re right all the time, but God thoroughly examines our motives.
21.3: It pleases God more when we demonstrate godliness and justice than when we merely offer him a sacrifice.
21.4: Arrogance, superiority, and pride are the fruits of sin.
21.5: Brilliant ideas pay off and bring you prosperity, but making hasty, impatient decisions will only lead to financial loss.
21.6: You can make a fortune dishonestly, but your crime will hold you in the snares of death!
21.7: Violent rebels don’t have a chance, for their rejection of truth and their love of evil will drag them deeper into darkness.
21.8: You can discern that a person is guilty by his devious actions and the innocence of a person by his honest, sincere ways.
21.9: It’s better to live all alone in a rickety shack than to share a castle with a crabby spouse!
21.10: The wicked always crave what is evil; they’ll show no mercy and get no mercy.
21.11: Senseless people learn their lessons the hard way, but the wise are teachable.
21.12: A godly, righteous person has the ability to bring the light of instruction to the wicked even though he despises what the wicked do.
21.13: If you close your heart to the cries of the poor, then I’ll close my ears when you cry out to me!
21.14: Try giving a secret gift to the one who is angry with you and watch his anger disappear. A kind, generous gift goes a long way to soothe the anger of one who is livid.
21.15: When justice is served, the lovers of God celebrate and rejoice, but the wicked begin to panic.
21.16: When you forsake the ways of wisdom, you will wander into the realm of dark spirits.
21.17: To love pleasure for pleasure’s sake will introduce you to poverty. Indulging in a life of luxury will never make you wealthy.
21.18: The wicked bring on themselves the very suffering they planned for others, for their treachery comes back to haunt them.
21.19: It’s better to live in a hut in the wilderness than with a crabby, scolding spouse!
21.20: In wisdom’s house you’ll find delightful treasures and the oil of the Holy Spirit. But the stupid squander what they’ve been given.
21.21: The lovers of God who chase after righteousness will find all their dreams come true: an abundant life drenched with favor and a fountain that overflows with satisfaction.
21.22: A warrior filled with wisdom ascends into the high place and releases breakthrough, bringing down the strongholds of the mighty.
21.23: Watch your words and be careful what you say, and you’ll be surprised by how few troubles you’ll have.
21.24: An arrogant man is inflated with pride— nothing but a snooty scoffer in love with his own opinion. Mr. Mocker is his name!
21.25: Taking the easy way out is the habit of a lazy man, and it will be his downfall. All day long he thinks about all the things that he craves, for he hasn’t learned the secret that the generous man has learned: extravagant giving never leads to poverty.
21.26: They are always greedy for more, while the godly love to give!
21.27: To bring an offering to God with an ulterior motive is detestable, for it amounts to nothing but hypocrisy.
21.28: No one believes a notorious liar, but the guarded words of an honest man stand the test of time.
21.29: The wicked are shameless and stubborn, but the lovers of God have a holy confidence.
21.30: All your brilliant wisdom and clever insight will be of no help at all if the Lord is against you.
21.31: You can do your best to prepare for the battle, but ultimate victory comes from the Lord God.

22.1: A beautiful reputation is more to be desired than great riches, and to be esteemed by others is more honorable than to own immense investments.
22.2: The rich and the poor have one thing in common: the Lord God created each one.
22.3: A prudent person with insight foresees danger coming and prepares himself for it. But the senseless rush blindly forward and suffer the consequences.
22.4: Laying your life down in tender surrender before the Lord will bring life, prosperity, and honor as your reward.
22.5: Twisted and perverse lives are surrounded by demonic influence. If you value your soul, stay far away from them.
22.6: Dedicate your children to God and point them in the way that they should go, and the values they’ve learned from you will be with them for life.
22.7: If you borrow money with interest, you’ll end up serving the interests of your creditors, for the rich rule over the poor.
22.8: Sin is a seed that brings a harvest; you’ll reap a heap of trouble with every seed you plant. For your investment in sins pays a full return— the full punishment you deserve!
22.9: When you are generous to the poor, you are enriched with blessings in return.
22.10: Say goodbye to a troublemaker and you’ll say goodbye to quarrels, strife, tension, and arguments, for a troublemaker traffics in shame.
22.11: The Lord loves those whose hearts are holy, and he is the friend of those whose ways are pure.
22.12: God passionately watches over his deep reservoir of revelation-knowledge, but he subverts the lies of those who pervert the truth.
22.13: A slacker always has an excuse for not working— like “I can’t go to work. There’s a lion outside! And murderers too! ”
22.14: Sex with an adulteress is like falling into the abyss. Those under God’s curse jump right in to their own destruction.
22.15: Although rebellion is woven into a young man’s heart, tough discipline can make him into a man.
22.16: There are two kinds of people headed toward poverty: those who exploit the poor and those who bribe the rich.
22.17: Listen carefully and open your heart. Drink in the wise revelation that I impart.
22.18: You’ll become winsome and wise when you treasure the beauty of my words. And always be prepared to share them at the appropriate time.
22.19: For I’m releasing these words to you this day, yes, even to you, so that your living hope will be found in God alone, for he is the only one who is always true.
22.20: Pay attention to these excellent sayings of three-fold things. For within my words you will discover true and reliable revelation. They will give you serenity so that you can reveal the truth of the word of the one who sends you.
22.21: In this way, you may know the truth and bring an accurate report to those who sent you.
22.22: Never oppress the poor or pass laws with the motive of crushing the weak.
22.23: For the Lord will rise to plead their case and humiliate the one who humiliates the poor.
22.24: Walk away from an angry man or you’ll embrace a snare in your soul by becoming bad-tempered just like him.
22.25: or you will learn to be like them and endanger your soul.
22.26: Why would you ever guarantee a loan for someone else or promise to be responsible for someone’s debts?
22.27: For if you fail to pay you could lose your shirt!
22.28: The previous generation has set boundaries in place. Don’t you dare move them just to benefit yourself.
22.29: If you are uniquely gifted in your work, you will rise and be promoted. You won’t be held back— you’ll stand before kings!

23.1: When you’ve been invited to dine with a very important leader, consider your manners and keep in mind whom you’re with.
23.2: Be careful to curb your appetite and catch yourself before you fall into the trap of wanting all you see.
23.3: Don’t crave their delicacies, for they may have another motive in having you sit at their table.
23.4: Don’t compare yourself to the rich. Surrender your selfish ambition and evaluate them properly.
23.5: For no sooner do you start counting your wealth than it sprouts wings and flies away like an eagle in the sky— here today, gone tomorrow!
23.6: Be sensible when you dine with a stingy man and don’t eat more than you should.
23.7: For as he thinks within himself, so is he. He will grudgingly say, “Go ahead and eat all you want,” but in his heart he resents the fact that he has to pay for your meal.
23.8: You’ll be sorry you ate anything at all, and all your compliments will be wasted.
23.9: A rebellious fool will despise your wise advice, so don’t even waste your time—save your breath!
23.10: Never move a long-standing boundary line or attempt to take land that belongs to the fatherless.
23.11: For they have a mighty protector, a loving redeemer, who watches over them, and he will stand up for their cause.
23.12: Pay close attention to the teaching that corrects you, and open your heart to every word of instruction.
23.13: Don’t withhold appropriate discipline from your child. Go ahead and punish him when he needs it. Don’t worry—it won’t kill him!
23.14: A good spanking could be the very thing that teaches him a lifelong lesson!
23.15: My beloved child, when your heart is full of wisdom, my heart is full of gladness.
23.16: And when you speak anointed words, we are speaking mouth to mouth!
23.17: Don’t allow the actions of evil men to cause you to burn with anger. Instead, burn with unrelenting passion as you worship God in holy awe.
23.18: Your future is bright and filled with a living hope that will never fade away.
23.19: As you listen to me, my beloved child, you will grow in wisdom and your heart will be drawn into understanding, which will empower you to make right decisions.
23.20: Don’t live in the excesses of drunkenness or gluttony, or waste your life away by partying all the time,
23.21: because drunkards and gluttons sleep their lives away and end up broke!
23.22: Give respect to your father and mother, for without them you wouldn’t even be here. And don’t neglect them when they grow old.
23.23: Embrace the truth and hold it close. Don’t let go of wisdom, instruction, and life-giving understanding.
23.24: When a father observes his child living in godliness, he is ecstatic with joy—nothing makes him prouder!
23.25: So may your father’s heart burst with joy and your mother’s soul be filled with gladness because of you.
23.26: My son, give me your heart and embrace fully what I’m about to tell you.
23.27: Stay far away from prostitutes and you’ll stay far away from the pit of destruction. For sleeping with a promiscuous woman is like falling into a trap that you’ll never be able to escape!
23.28: Like a robber hiding in the shadows she’s waiting to claim another victim— another husband unfaithful to his wife.
23.29: Who has anguish? Who has bitter sorrow? Who constantly complains and argues? Who stumbles and falls and hurts himself? Who’s the one with bloodshot eyes?
23.30: It’s the one who drinks too much and is always looking for a brew. Make sure it’s never you!
23.31: And don’t be drunk with wine but be known as one who enjoys the company of the lovers of God,
23.32: for drunkenness brings the sting of a serpent, like the fangs of a viper spreading poison into your soul.
23.33: It will make you hallucinate, mumble, and speak words that are perverse.
23.34: You’ll be like a seasick sailor being tossed to and fro, dizzy and out of your mind.
23.35: You’ll awake only to say, “What hit me? I feel like I’ve been run over by a truck!” Yet off you’ll go, looking for another drink!

24.1: Don’t envy the wealth of the wicked or crave their company.
24.2: For they’re obsessed with causing trouble and their conversations are corrupt.
24.3: Wise people are builders — they build families, businesses, communities. And through intelligence and insight their enterprises are established and endure.
24.4: Because of their skilled leadership, the hearts of people are filled with the treasures of wisdom and the pleasures of spiritual wealth.
24.5: Wisdom can make anyone into a mighty warrior, and revelation-knowledge increases strength.
24.6: Wise strategy is necessary to wage war, and with many astute advisers you’ll see the path to victory more clearly.
24.7: Wisdom is a treasure too lofty for a quarreling fool — he’ll have nothing to say when leaders gather together.
24.8: There is one who makes plans to do evil— Master Schemer is his name.
24.9: If you plan to do evil, it’s as wrong as doing it. And everyone detests a troublemaker.
24.10: If you faint when under pressure, you have need of courage.
24.11: Go and rescue the perishing! Be their savior! Why would you stand back and watch them stagger to their death?
24.12: And why would you say, “But it’s none of my business”? The one who knows you completely and judges your every motive is also the keeper of souls—and not just yours! He sees through your excuses and holds you responsible for failing to help those whose lives are threatened.
24.13: Revelation-knowledge is a delicacy, sweet like flowing honey that melts in your mouth. Eat as much of it as you can, my friend!
24.14: For then you will perceive what is true wisdom, your future will be bright, and this hope living within you will never disappoint you.
24.15: Listen up, you wicked, irreverent ones— don’t harass the lovers of God and don’t invade their resting place.
24.16: For the lovers of God may suffer adversity and stumble seven times, but they will continue to rise over and over again. But the unrighteous are brought down by just one calamity and will never be able to rise again.
24.17: Never gloat when your enemy meets disaster, and don’t be quick to rejoice if he falls.
24.18: For the Lord, who sees your heart, will be displeased with you and will pity your foe.
24.19: Don’t be angrily offended over evildoers or be agitated by them.
24.20: For the wicked have no life and no future— their light of life will die out.
24.21: My child, stand in awe of Yahweh! Give counsel to others, but don’t mingle with those who are rebellious.
24.22: For sudden destruction will fall upon them and their lives will be ruined in a moment. And who knows what retribution they will face!
24.23: Those enlightened with wisdom have spoken these proverbs: Judgment must be impartial, for it is always wrong to be swayed by a person’s status.
24.24: If you say to the guilty, “You are innocent,” the nation will curse you and the people will revile you.
24.25: But when you convict the guilty, the people will thank you and reward you with favor.
24.26: Speaking honestly is a sign of true friendship.
24.27: Go ahead, build your career and give yourself to your work. But if you put me first, you’ll see your family built up!
24.28: Why would you be a false accuser and slander with your words?
24.29: Don’t ever spitefully say, “I’ll get even with him! I’ll do to him what he did to me!”
24.30: One day I passed by the field of a lazy man, and I noticed the vineyards of a slacker. I observed nothing but thorns, weeds, and broken-down walls.
24.31: I saw that it was overgrown with thorns. It was covered with weeds, and its walls were broken down.
24.32: So I considered their lack of wisdom, and I pondered the lessons I could learn from this:
24.33: Professional work habits prevent poverty from becoming your permanent business partner. And: If you put off until tomorrow the work you could do today, tomorrow never seems to come.
24.34: and poverty will pounce on you like a bandit; scarcity will attack you like an armed robber.

25.1: Solomon’s proverbs, published by the scribes of King Hezekiah:
25.2: God conceals the revelation of his word in the hiding place of his glory. But the honor of kings is revealed by how they thoroughly search out the deeper meaning of all that God says.
25.3: The heart of a king is full of understanding, like the heavens are high and the ocean is deep.
25.4: If you burn away the impurities from silver, a sterling vessel will emerge from the fire.
25.5: And if you purge corruption from the kingdom, a king’s reign will be established in righteousness.
25.6: Don’t boast in the presence of a king or promote yourself by taking a seat at the head table and pretending that you’re someone important.
25.7: For it is better for the king to say to you, “Come, you should sit at the head table,” than for him to say in front of everyone, “Please get up and move— you’re sitting in the place of the prince.”
25.8: Don’t be hasty to file a lawsuit. By starting something you wish you hadn’t, you could be humiliated when you lose your case.
25.9: Don’t reveal another person’s secret just to prove a point in an argument, or you could be accused of being a gossip
25.10: and gain a reputation for being one who betrays the confidence of a friend.
25.11: Winsome words spoken at just the right time are as appealing as apples gilded in gold surrounded with silver.
25.12: When you humbly receive wise correction, it adorns your life with beauty and makes you a better person.
25.13: A reliable, trustworthy messenger refreshes the heart of his master, like a gentle snowfall at harvest time.
25.14: Clouds that carry no water and a wind that brings no refreshing rain — that’s what you’re like when you boast of a gift that you don’t have.
25.15: Use patience and kindness when you want to persuade leaders and watch them change their minds right in front of you. For your gentle wisdom will quell the strongest resistance.
25.16: When you discover something sweet, don’t overindulge and eat more than you need, for excess in anything can make you sick of even a good thing.
25.17: Don’t wear out your welcome by staying too long at the home of your friends, or they may get fed up with always having you there and wish you hadn’t come.
25.18: Lying about and slandering people are as bad as hitting them with a club, or wounding them with an arrow, or stabbing them with a sword.
25.19: You can’t depend on an unreliable person when you really need help. It can be compared to biting down on an abscessed tooth or walking with a sprained ankle.
25.20: When you sing a song of joy to someone suffering in the deepest grief and heartache, it can be compared to disrobing in the middle of a blizzard or rubbing salt in a wound.
25.21: Is your enemy hungry? Buy him lunch. Win him over with your kindness.
25.22: Your surprising generosity will awaken his conscience and God will reward you with favor.
25.23: As the north wind brings a storm, saying things you shouldn’t brings a storm to any relationship.
25.24: It’s better to live all alone in a rundown shack than to share a castle with a crabby spouse!
25.25: Like a drink of cool water refreshes a weary, thirsty soul, so hearing good news revives the spirit.
25.26: When a lover of God gives in and compromises with wickedness, it can be compared to contaminating a stream with sewage or polluting a fountain.
25.27: It’s good to eat sweet things, but you can take too much. It’s good to be honored, but to seek words of praise is not honor at all.
25.28: If you live without restraint and are unable to control your temper, you’re as helpless as a city with broken-down defenses, open to attack.

26.1: It is totally out of place to promote and honor a fool, just like it’s out of place to have snow in the summer and rain at harvest time.
26.2: An undeserved curse will be powerless to harm you. It may flutter over you like a bird, but it will find no place to land.
26.3: Guide a horse with a whip, direct a donkey with a bridle, and lead a rebellious fool with a beating on his backside!
26.4: Don’t respond to the words of a fool with more foolish words, or you will become as foolish as he is!
26.5: Instead, if you’re asked a silly question, answer it with words of wisdom so the fool doesn’t think he’s so clever.
26.6: If you choose a fool to represent you, you’re asking for trouble. It will be as bad for you as cutting off your own feet!
26.7: You can never trust the words of a fool, just like a crippled man can’t trust his legs to support him.
26.8: Give honor to a fool and watch it backfire— like a stone tied to a slingshot.
26.9: The statements of a fool will hurt others like a thorn bush brandished by a drunk.
26.10: Like a reckless archer shooting arrows at random is the impatient employer who hires just any fool who comes along— someone’s going to get hurt!
26.11: Fools are famous for repeating their errors, like dogs are known to return to their vomit.
26.12: There’s only one thing worse than a fool, and that’s the smug, conceited man always in love with his own opinions.
26.13: The lazy loafer says, “I can’t go out and look for a job— there may be a lion out there roaming wild in the streets!”
26.14: As a door is hinged to the wall, so the lazy man keeps turning over, hinged to his bed!
26.15: There are some people so lazy they won’t even work to feed themselves.
26.16: A self-righteous person is convinced he’s smarter than seven wise counselors who tell him the truth.
26.17: It’s better to grab a stray dog by its ears than to meddle in a quarrel that’s none of your business.
26.18: The one who is caught lying to his friend, who says, “I didn’t mean it, I was only joking,” can be compared to a madman randomly shooting off deadly weapons.
26.19: is someone who lies to a friend and then says, "I was only joking."
26.20: It takes fuel to have a fire— a fire dies down when you run out of fuel. So quarrels disappear when the gossip ends.
26.21: Add fuel to the fire and the blaze goes on. So add an argumentative man to the mix, and you’ll keep strife alive.
26.22: Gossip is so delicious, and how we love to swallow it! For slander is easily absorbed into our innermost being.
26.23: Smooth talk can hide a corrupt heart just like a pretty glaze covers a cheap clay pot.
26.24: Kind words can be a cover to conceal hatred of others, for hypocrisy loves to hide behind flattery.
26.25: So don’t be drawn in by the hypocrite, for his gracious speech is a charade, nothing but a masquerade covering his hatred and evil on parade.
26.26: Don’t worry—he can’t keep the mask on for long. One day his hypocrisy will be exposed before all the world.
26.27: Go ahead, set a trap for others— and then watch as it snaps back on you! Start a landslide and you’ll be the one who gets crushed.
26.28: Hatred is the root of slander and insecurity the root of flattery.

27.1: Never brag about the plans you have for tomorrow, for you don’t have a clue what tomorrow may bring to you.
27.2: Let someone else honor you for your accomplishments, for self-praise is never appropriate.
27.3: It’s easier to carry a heavy boulder and a ton of sand than to be provoked by a fool and have to carry that burden!
27.4: The rage and anger of others can be overwhelming, but it’s nothing compared to jealousy’s fire.
27.5: It’s better to be corrected openly if it stems from hidden love.
27.6: You can trust a friend who wounds you with his honesty, but your enemy’s pretended flattery comes from insincerity.
27.7: When your soul is full, you turn down even the sweetest honey. But when your soul is starving, every bitter thing becomes sweet.
27.8: Like a bird that has fallen from its nest is the one who is dislodged from his home.
27.9: Sweet friendships refresh the soul and awaken our hearts with joy, for good friends are like the anointing oil that yields the fragrant incense of God’s presence.
27.10: So never give up on a friend or abandon a friend of your father— for in the day of your brokenness you won’t have to run to a relative for help. A friend nearby is better than a relative far away.
27.11: My son, when you walk in wisdom, my heart is filled with gladness, for the way you live is proof that I’ve not taught you in vain.
27.12: A wise, shrewd person discerns the danger ahead and prepares himself, but the naïve simpleton never looks ahead and suffers the consequences.
27.13: Cosign for one you barely know and you will pay a great price! Anyone stupid enough to guarantee the loan of another deserves to have his property seized in payment.
27.14: Do you think you’re blessing your neighbors when you sing at the top of your lungs early in the morning? Don’t be fooled— they’ll curse you for doing it!
27.15: An endless drip, drip, drip, from a leaky faucet and the words of a cranky, nagging wife have the same effect.
27.16: Can you stop the north wind from blowing or grasp a handful of oil? That’s easier than to stop her from complaining.
27.17: It takes a grinding wheel to sharpen a blade, and so one person sharpens the character of another.
27.18: Tend an orchard and you’ll have fruit to eat. Serve the Master’s interests and you’ll receive honor that’s sweet.
27.19: Just as no two faces are exactly alike, so every heart is different.
27.20: Death and destruction are never filled, and the desires of men’s hearts are insatiable.
27.21: Fire is the way to test the purity of silver and gold, but the character of a man is tested by giving him a measure of fame.
27.22: You can beat a fool half to death and still never beat the foolishness out of him.
27.23: A shepherd should pay close attention to the faces of his flock and hold close to his heart the condition of those he cares for.
27.24: A man’s strength, power, and riches will one day fade away; not even nations endure forever.
27.25: Take care of your responsibilities and be diligent in your business and you will have more than enough— an abundance of food, clothing, and plenty for your household.
27.26: your sheep will provide wool for clothing, and your goats will be sold for the price of a field.
27.27: And you will have enough goats' milk for you, your family, and your servants.

28.1: Guilty criminals experience paranoia even though no one threatens them. But the innocent lovers of God, because of righteousness, will have the boldness of a young, ferocious lion!
28.2: A rebellious nation is thrown into chaos, but leaders anointed with wisdom will restore law and order.
28.3: When a pauper oppresses the destitute, it’s like a flash flood that sweeps away their last hope.
28.4: Those who turn their backs on what they know is right will no longer be able to tell right from wrong. But those who love the truth strengthen their souls.
28.5: Justice never makes sense to men devoted to darkness, but those tenderly devoted to the Lord can understand justice perfectly.
28.6: It’s more respectable to be poor and pure than rich and perverse.
28.7: To be obedient to what you’ve been taught proves you’re an honorable child, but to socialize with the lawless brings shame to your parents.
28.8: Go ahead and get rich on the backs of the poor, but all the wealth you gather will one day be given to those who are kind to the needy.
28.9: If you close your heart and refuse to listen to God’s instruction, even your prayer will be despised.
28.10: Those who tempt the lovers of God with an evil scheme will fall into their own traps. But the innocent who resist temptation will experience reward.
28.11: The wealthy in their conceit presume to be wise, but a poor person with discernment can see right through them.
28.12: The triumphant joy of God’s lovers releases great glory. But when the wicked rise to power, everyone goes into hiding.
28.13: If you cover up your sin you’ll never do well. But if you confess your sins and forsake them, you will be kissed by mercy.
28.14: Overjoyed is the one who with tender heart trembles before God, but the stubborn, unyielding heart will experience even greater evil.
28.15: Ruthless rulers can only be compared to raging lions and roaming bears.
28.16: Abusive leaders fail to employ wisdom, but leaders who despise corruption will enjoy a long and full life.
28.17: A murderer’s conscience will torment him— a fugitive haunted by guilt all the way to the grave with no one to support him.
28.18: The pure will be rescued from failure, but the perverse will suddenly fall into ruin.
28.19: Work hard and you’ll have all you desire, but chase a fantasy and you could end up with nothing.
28.20: Life’s blessings drench the honest and faithful person, but punishment rains down upon the greedy and dishonest.
28.21: Giving favoritism to the rich and powerful is disgusting, and this is done by the type of judge who would betray a man for a bribe.
28.22: A greedy man is in a race to get rich, but he forgets that he could lose what’s most important and end up with nothing.
28.23: If you correct someone with constructive criticism, in the end he will appreciate it more than flattery.
28.24: A person who would reject his own parents and say, “What’s wrong with that?” is as bad as a murderer.
28.25: To make rash, hasty decisions shows that you are not trusting the Lord. But when you rely totally on God, you will still act carefully and prudently.
28.26: Self-confident know-it-alls will prove to be fools. But when you lean on the wisdom from above, you will have a way to escape the troubles of your own making.
28.27: You will never go without if you give to the poor. But if you’re heartless, stingy, and selfish, you invite curses upon yourself.
28.28: When wicked leaders rise to power, good people go into hiding. But when they fall from power, the godly take their place.

29.1: Stubborn people who repeatedly refuse to accept correction will suddenly be broken and never recover.
29.2: Everyone rejoices when the lovers of God flourish, but the people groan when the wicked rise to power.
29.3: When you love wisdom, your father is overjoyed. But when you associate with prostitutes, you waste your wealth in exchange for disgrace.
29.4: A godly leader who values justice is a great strength and example to the people. But the one who sells his influence for money tears down what is right.
29.5: Flattery can often be used as a trap to hide ulterior motives and take advantage of you.
29.6: The wicked always have a trap laid for others, but the lovers of God escape as they sing and shout in joyous triumph!
29.7: God’s righteous people will pour themselves out for the poor, but the ungodly make no attempt to understand or help the needy.
29.8: Arrogant cynics love to pick fights, but the humble and wise love to pursue peace.
29.9: There’s no use arguing with a fool, for his ranting and raving prevent you from making a case and settling the argument in a calm way.
29.10: Violent men hate those with integrity, but the lovers of God esteem those who are holy.
29.11: You can recognize fools by the way they give full vent to their rage and let their words fly! But the wise bite their tongues and hold back all they could say.
29.12: When leaders listen to false accusations, their associates become scoundrels.
29.13: Poor people and their oppressors have only one thing in common— God made them both.
29.14: The best insurance for a leader’s longevity is to demonstrate justice for the poor.
29.15: Experiencing many corrections and rebukes will make you wise. But if left to your own ways, you’ll bring disgrace to your parents.
29.16: When the wicked are in power, lawlessness abounds. But the patient lovers of God will one day watch in triumph as their stronghold topples!
29.17: Correct your child and one day you’ll find he has changed and will bring you great delight.
29.18: When there is no clear prophetic vision, people quickly wander astray. But when you follow the revelation of the Word, heaven’s bliss fills your soul.
29.19: A stubborn servant can’t be corrected by words alone. For even if he understands, he pays no attention to you.
29.20: There’s only one kind of person who is worse than a fool: the impetuous one who speaks without thinking first.
29.21: If you pamper your servants, don’t be surprised when they expect to be treated as sons.
29.22: The source of strife is found in an angry heart, for sin surrounds the life of a furious man.
29.23: Lift yourself up with pride and you will soon be brought low, but a meek and humble spirit will add to your honor.
29.24: You are your own worst enemy when you partner with a thief, for a curse of guilt will come upon you when you fail to report a crime.
29.25: Fear and intimidation is a trap that holds you back. But when you place your confidence in the Lord, you will be seated in the high place.
29.26: Everyone curries favor with leaders. But God is the judge, and justice comes from him.
29.27: The wicked hate those who live a godly life, but the righteous hate injustice wherever it’s found.

30.1: These are the collected sayings of the prophet Agur, Jakeh’s son — the amazing revelation he imparted to Ithiel and Ukal.
30.2: God, I’m so weary and worn out, I feel more like a beast than a man. I was made in your image, but I lack understanding.
30.3: I’ve yet to learn the wisdom that comes from the full and intimate knowledge of you, the Holy One.
30.4: Who is it that travels back and forth from the heavenly realm to the earth? Who controls the wind as it blows and holds it in his fists? Who tucks the rain into the cloak of his clouds? Who stretches out the skyline from one vista to the other? What is his name? And what is the name of his Son? Who can tell me?
30.5: Every promise from the faithful God is pure and proves to be true. He is a wraparound shield of protection for all his lovers who run to hide in him.
30.6: Never add to his words, or he will have to rebuke you and prove that you’re a liar.
30.7: God, there are two things I’m asking you for before I die, only two:
30.8: Empty out of my heart everything that is false— every lie, and every crooked thing. And give me neither undue poverty nor undue wealth— but rather, feed my soul with the measure of prosperity that pleases you.
30.9: May my satisfaction be found in you. Don’t let me be so rich that I don’t need you or so poor that I have to resort to dishonesty just to make ends meet. Then my life will never detract from bringing glory to your name.
30.10: Never defame a servant before his master, for you will be the guilty one and a curse will come upon you.
30.11: There is a generation rising that curses their fathers and speaks evil of their mothers.
30.12: There is a generation rising that considers themselves to be pure in their own eyes, yet they are morally filthy, unwashed, and unclean.
30.13: There is a generation rising that is so filled with pride, they think they are superior and look down on others.
30.14: There is a generation rising that uses their words like swords to cut and slash those who are different. They would devour the poor, the needy, and the afflicted from off the face of the earth!
30.15: There are three words to describe the greedy: “Give me more!” There are some things that are never satisfied. Forever craving more, they’re unable to say, “That’s enough!” Here are four:
30.16: the grave, yawning for another victim, the barren womb, ever wanting a child, thirsty soil, ever longing for rain, and a raging fire, devouring its fuel. They’re all insatiable.
30.17: The eye that mocks his father and dishonors his elderly mother deserves to be plucked out by the ravens of the valley and fed to the young vultures!
30.18: There are four marvelous mysteries that are too amazing to unravel — who could fully explain them?
30.19: The way an eagle flies in the sky, the way a snake glides on a boulder, the path of a ship as it passes through the sea, and the way a bridegroom falls in love with his bride.
30.20: Here is the deceptive way of the adulterous woman: she takes what she wants and then says, “I’ve done nothing wrong.”
30.21: There are four intolerable events that are simply unbearable to observe:
30.22: when an unfaithful servant becomes a ruler, when a scoundrel comes into great wealth,
30.23: when an unfaithful woman marries a good man, and when a mistress replaces a faithful wife.
30.24: The earth has four creatures that are very small but very wise:
30.25: The feeble ant has little strength, yet look how it diligently gathers its food in the summer to last throughout the winter.
30.26: The delicate rock-badger isn’t all that strong, yet look how it makes a secure home, nestled in the rocks.
30.27: The locusts have no king to lead them, yet they cooperate as they move forward by bands.
30.28: And the small lizard is easy to catch as it clings to the walls with its hands, yet it can be found inside a king’s palace.
30.29: There are four stately monarchs who are impressive to watch as they go forth:
30.30: the lion, the king of the jungle, who is afraid of no one,
30.31: the rooster strutting boldly among the hens, the male goat out in front leading the herd, and a king leading his regal procession.
30.32: If you’ve acted foolishly by drawing attention to yourself, or if you’ve thought about saying something stupid, you’d better shut your mouth.
30.33: For such stupidity may give you a bloody nose! Stirring up an argument only leads to an angry confrontation.

31.1: King Lemuel’s royal words of wisdom: These are the inspired words my mother taught me.
31.2: Listen, my dear son, son of my womb. You are the answer to my prayers, my son.
31.3: So keep yourself sexually pure from the promiscuous, wayward woman. Don’t waste the strength of your anointing on those who ruin kings— you’ll live to regret it!
31.4: For you are a king, Lemuel, and it’s never fitting for a king to be drunk on wine or for rulers to crave alcohol.
31.5: For when they drink they forget justice and ignore the rights of those in need, those who depend on them for leadership.
31.6: Strong drink is given to the terminally ill, who are suffering at the brink of death. Wine is for those in depression in order to drown their sorrows. Let them drink and forget their poverty and misery.
31.7: Let them drink to forget their poverty and remember their troubles no more.
31.8: But you are to be a king who speaks up on behalf of the disenfranchised and pleads for the legal rights of the defenseless and those who are dying.
31.9: Be a righteous king, judging on behalf of the poor and interceding for those most in need.
31.10: Who could ever find a wife like this one — she is a woman of strength and mighty valor! She’s full of wealth and wisdom. The price paid for her was greater than many jewels.
31.11: Her husband has entrusted his heart to her, for she brings him the rich spoils of victory.
31.12: All throughout her life she brings him what is good and not evil.
31.13: She searches out continually to possess that which is pure and righteous. She delights in the work of her hands.
31.14: She gives out revelation-truth to feed others. She is like a trading ship bringing divine supplies from the merchant.
31.15: Even in the night season she arises and sets food on the table for hungry ones in her house and for others.
31.16: She sets her heart upon a field and takes it as her own. She labors there to plant the living vines.
31.17: She wraps herself in strength, might, and power in all her works.
31.18: She tastes and experiences a better substance, and her shining light will not be extinguished, no matter how dark the night.
31.19: She stretches out her hands to help the needy and she lays hold of the wheels of government.
31.20: She is known by her extravagant generosity to the poor, for she always reaches out her hands to those in need.
31.21: She is not afraid of tribulation, for all her household is covered in the dual garments of righteousness and grace.
31.22: Her clothing is beautifully knit together — a purple gown of exquisite linen.
31.23: Her husband is famous and admired by all, sitting as the venerable judge of his people.
31.24: Even her works of righteousness she does for the benefit of her enemies.
31.25: Bold power and glorious majesty are wrapped around her as she laughs with joy over the latter days.
31.26: Her teachings are filled with wisdom and kindness as loving instruction pours from her lips.
31.27: She watches over the ways of her household and meets every need they have.
31.28: Her sons and daughters arise in one accord to extol her virtues, and her husband arises to speak of her in glowing terms.
31.29: “There are many valiant and noble ones, but you have ascended above them all!”
31.30: Charm can be misleading, and beauty is vain and so quickly fades, but this virtuous woman lives in the wonder, awe, and fear of the Lord. She will be praised throughout eternity.
31.31: So go ahead and give her the credit that is due, for she has become a radiant woman, and all her loving works of righteousness deserve to be admired at the gateways of every city!

1.1: These are the words of the Teacher, King David's son, who ruled in Jerusalem.
1.2: "Everything is meaningless," says the Teacher, "utterly meaningless!"
1.3: What do people get for all their hard work?
1.4: Generations come and go, but nothing really changes.
1.5: The sun rises and sets and hurries around to rise again.
1.6: The wind blows south and north, here and there, twisting back and forth, getting nowhere.
1.7: The rivers run into the sea, but the sea is never full. Then the water returns again to the rivers and flows again to the sea.
1.8: Everything is so weary and tiresome! No matter how much we see, we are never satisfied. No matter how much we hear, we are not content.
1.9: History merely repeats itself. It has all been done before. Nothing under the sun is truly new.
1.10: What can you point to that is new? How do you know it didn't already exist long ago?
1.11: We don't remember what happened in those former times. And in future generations, no one will remember what we are doing now.
1.12: I, the Teacher, was king of Israel, and I lived in Jerusalem.
1.13: I devoted myself to search for understanding and to explore by wisdom everything being done in the world. I soon discovered that God has dealt a tragic existence to the human race.
1.14: Everything under the sun is meaningless, like chasing the wind.
1.15: What is wrong cannot be righted. What is missing cannot be recovered.
1.16: I said to myself, "Look, I am wiser than any of the kings who ruled in Jerusalem before me. I have greater wisdom and knowledge than any of them."
1.17: So I worked hard to distinguish wisdom from foolishness. But now I realize that even this was like chasing the wind.
1.18: For the greater my wisdom, the greater my grief. To increase knowledge only increases sorrow.

2.1: I said to myself, "Come now, let's give pleasure a try. Let's look for the `good things' in life." But I found that this, too, was meaningless.
2.2: "It is silly to be laughing all the time," I said. "What good does it do to seek only pleasure?"
2.3: After much thought, I decided to cheer myself with wine. While still seeking wisdom, I clutched at foolishness. In this way, I hoped to experience the only happiness most people find during their brief life in this world.
2.4: I also tried to find meaning by building huge homes for myself and by planting beautiful vineyards.
2.5: I made gardens and parks, filling them with all kinds of fruit trees.
2.6: I built reservoirs to collect the water to irrigate my many flourishing groves.
2.7: I bought slaves, both men and women, and others were born into my household. I also owned great herds and flocks, more than any of the kings who lived in Jerusalem before me.
2.8: I collected great sums of silver and gold, the treasure of many kings and provinces. I hired wonderful singers, both men and women, and had many beautiful concubines. I had everything a man could desire!
2.9: So I became greater than any of the kings who ruled in Jerusalem before me. And with it all, I remained clear-eyed so that I could evaluate all these things.
2.10: Anything I wanted, I took. I did not restrain myself from any joy. I even found great pleasure in hard work, an additional reward for all my labors.
2.11: But as I looked at everything I had worked so hard to accomplish, it was all so meaningless. It was like chasing the wind. There was nothing really worthwhile anywhere.
2.12: So I decided to compare wisdom and folly, and anyone else would come to the same conclusions I did.
2.13: Wisdom is of more value than foolishness, just as light is better than darkness.
2.14: For the wise person sees, while the fool is blind. Yet I saw that wise and foolish people share the same fate.
2.15: Both of them die. Just as the fool will die, so will I. So of what value is all my wisdom? Then I said to myself, "This is all so meaningless!"
2.16: For the wise person and the fool both die, and in the days to come, both will be forgotten.
2.17: So now I hate life because everything done here under the sun is so irrational. Everything is meaningless, like chasing the wind.
2.18: I am disgusted that I must leave the fruits of my hard work to others.
2.19: And who can tell whether my successors will be wise or foolish? And yet they will control everything I have gained by my skill and hard work. How meaningless!
2.20: So I turned in despair from hard work. It was not the answer to my search for satisfaction in this life.
2.21: For though I do my work with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, I must leave everything I gain to people who haven't worked to earn it. This is not only foolish but highly unfair.
2.22: So what do people get for all their hard work?
2.23: Their days of labor are filled with pain and grief; even at night they cannot rest. It is all utterly meaningless.
2.24: So I decided there is nothing better than to enjoy food and drink and to find satisfaction in work. Then I realized that this pleasure is from the hand of God.
2.25: For who can eat or enjoy anything apart from him?
2.26: God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to those who please him. But if a sinner becomes wealthy, God takes the wealth away and gives it to those who please him. Even this, however, is meaningless, like chasing the wind.

3.1: 1 There is a time for everything, a season for every activity under heaven.
3.2: A time to be born and a time to die. A time to plant and a time to harvest.
3.3: A time to kill and a time to heal. A time to tear down and a time to rebuild.
3.4: A time to cry and a time to laugh. A time to grieve and a time to dance.
3.5: A time to scatter stones and a time to gather stones. A time to embrace and a time to turn away.
3.6: A time to search and a time to lose. A time to keep and a time to throw away.
3.7: A time to tear and a time to mend. A time to be quiet and a time to speak up.
3.8: A time to love and a time to hate. A time for war and a time for peace.
3.9: What do people really get for all their hard work?
3.10: I have thought about this in connection with the various kinds of work God has given people to do.
3.11: God has made everything beautiful for its own time. He has planted eternity in the human heart, but even so, people cannot see the whole scope of God's work from beginning to end.
3.12: So I concluded that there is nothing better for people than to be happy and to enjoy themselves as long as they can.
3.13: And people should eat and drink and enjoy the fruits of their labor, for these are gifts from God.
3.14: And I know that whatever God does is final. Nothing can be added to it or taken from it. God's purpose in this is that people should fear him.
3.15: Whatever exists today and whatever will exist in the future has already existed in the past. For God calls each event back in its turn.
3.16: I also noticed that throughout the world there is evil in the courtroom. Yes, even the courts of law are corrupt!
3.17: I said to myself, "In due season God will judge everyone, both good and bad, for all their deeds."
3.18: Then I realized that God allows people to continue in their sinful ways so he can test them. That way, they can see for themselves that they are no better than animals.
3.19: For humans and animals both breathe the same air, and both die. So people have no real advantage over the animals. How meaningless!
3.20: Both go to the same place--the dust from which they came and to which they must return.
3.21: For who can prove that the human spirit goes upward and the spirit of animals goes downward into the earth?
3.22: So I saw that there is nothing better for people than to be happy in their work. That is why they are here! No one will bring them back from death to enjoy life in the future.

4.1: Again I observed all the oppression that takes place in our world. I saw the tears of the oppressed, with no one to comfort them. The oppressors have great power, and the victims are helpless.
4.2: So I concluded that the dead are better off than the living.
4.3: And most fortunate of all are those who were never born. For they have never seen all the evil that is done in our world.
4.4: Then I observed that most people are motivated to success by their envy of their neighbors. But this, too, is meaningless, like chasing the wind.
4.5: Foolish people refuse to work and almost starve.
4.6: They feel it is better to be lazy and barely survive than to work hard, especially when in the long run everything is so futile.
4.7: I observed yet another example of meaninglessness in our world.
4.8: This is the case of a man who is all alone, without a child or a brother, yet who works hard to gain as much wealth as he can. But then he asks himself, "Who am I working for? Why am I giving up so much pleasure now?" It is all so meaningless and depressing.
4.9: Two people can accomplish more than twice as much as one; they get a better return for their labor.
4.10: If one person falls, the other can reach out and help. But people who are alone when they fall are in real trouble.
4.11: And on a cold night, two under the same blanket can gain warmth from each other. But how can one be warm alone?
4.12: A person standing alone can be attacked and defeated, but two can stand back-to-back and conquer. Three are even better, for a triple-braided cord is not easily broken.
4.13: It is better to be a poor but wise youth than to be an old and foolish king who refuses all advice.
4.14: Such a youth could come from prison and succeed. He might even become king, though he was born in poverty.
4.15: Everyone is eager to help such a youth, even to help him take the throne.
4.16: He might become the leader of millions and be very popular. But then the next generation grows up and rejects him! So again, it is all meaningless, like chasing the wind.

5.1: As you enter the house of God, keep your ears open and your mouth shut! Don't be a fool who doesn't realize that mindless offerings to God are evil.
5.2: And don't make rash promises to God, for he is in heaven, and you are only here on earth. So let your words be few.
5.3: Just as being too busy gives you nightmares, being a fool makes you a blabbermouth.
5.4: So when you make a promise to God, don't delay in following through, for God takes no pleasure in fools. Keep all the promises you make to him.
5.5: It is better to say nothing than to promise something that you don't follow through on.
5.6: In such cases, your mouth is making you sin. And don't defend yourself by telling the Temple messenger that the promise you made was a mistake. That would make God angry, and he might wipe out everything you have achieved.
5.7: Dreaming all the time instead of working is foolishness. And there is ruin in a flood of empty words. Fear God instead.
5.8: If you see a poor person being oppressed by the powerful and justice being miscarried throughout the land, don't be surprised! For every official is under orders from higher up, and matters of justice only get lost in red tape and bureaucracy.
5.9: Even the king milks the land for his own profit!
5.10: Those who love money will never have enough. How absurd to think that wealth brings true happiness!
5.11: The more you have, the more people come to help you spend it. So what is the advantage of wealth--except perhaps to watch it run through your fingers!
5.12: People who work hard sleep well, whether they eat little or much. But the rich are always worrying and seldom get a good night's sleep.
5.13: There is another serious problem I have seen in the world. Riches are sometimes hoarded to the harm of the saver,
5.14: or they are put into risky investments that turn sour, and everything is lost. In the end, there is nothing left to pass on to one's children.
5.15: People who live only for wealth come to the end of their lives as naked and empty-handed as on the day they were born.
5.16: And this, too, is a very serious problem. As people come into this world, so they depart. All their hard work is for nothing. They have been working for the wind, and everything will be swept away.
5.17: Throughout their lives, they live under a cloud--frustrated, discouraged, and angry.
5.18: Even so, I have noticed one thing, at least, that is good. It is good for people to eat well, drink a good glass of wine, and enjoy their work--whatever they do under the sun--for however long God lets them live.
5.19: And it is a good thing to receive wealth from God and the good health to enjoy it. To enjoy your work and accept your lot in life--that is indeed a gift from God.
5.20: People who do this rarely look with sorrow on the past, for God has given them reasons for joy.

6.1: There is another serious tragedy I have seen in our world.
6.2: God gives great wealth and honor to some people and gives them everything they could ever want, but then he doesn't give them the health to enjoy it. They die, and others get it all! This is meaningless--a sickening tragedy.
6.3: A man might have a hundred children and live to be very old. But if he finds no satisfaction in life and in the end does not even get a decent burial, I say he would have been better off born dead.
6.4: I realize that his birth would have been meaningless and ended in darkness. He wouldn't even have had a name,
6.5: and he would never have seen the sun or known of its existence. Yet he would have had more peace than he has in growing up to be an unhappy man.
6.6: He might live a thousand years twice over but not find contentment. And since he must die like everyone else--well, what's the use?
6.7: All people spend their lives scratching for food, but they never seem to have enough.
6.8: Considering this, do wise people really have any advantage over fools? Do poor people gain anything by being wise and knowing how to act in front of others?
6.9: Enjoy what you have rather than desiring what you don't have. Just dreaming about nice things is meaningless; it is like chasing the wind.
6.10: Everything has already been decided. It was known long ago what each person would be. So there's no use arguing with God about your destiny.
6.11: The more words you speak, the less they mean. So why overdo it?
6.12: In the few days of our empty lives, who knows how our days can best be spent? And who can tell what will happen in the future after we are gone?

7.1: A good reputation is more valuable than the most expensive perfume. In the same way, the day you die is better than the day you are born.
7.2: It is better to spend your time at funerals than at festivals. For you are going to die, and you should think about it while there is still time.
7.3: Sorrow is better than laughter, for sadness has a refining influence on us.
7.4: A wise person thinks much about death, while the fool thinks only about having a good time now.
7.5: It is better to be criticized by a wise person than to be praised by a fool!
7.6: Indeed, a fool's laughter is quickly gone, like thorns crackling in a fire. This also is meaningless.
7.7: Extortion turns wise people into fools, and bribes corrupt the heart.
7.8: Finishing is better than starting. Patience is better than pride.
7.9: Don't be quick-tempered, for anger is the friend of fools.
7.10: Don't long for "the good old days," for you don't know whether they were any better than today.
7.11: Being wise is as good as being rich; in fact, it is better.
7.12: Wisdom or money can get you almost anything, but it's important to know that only wisdom can save your life.
7.13: Notice the way God does things; then fall into line. Don't fight the ways of God, for who can straighten out what he has made crooked?
7.14: Enjoy prosperity while you can. But when hard times strike, realize that both come from God. That way you will realize that nothing is certain in this life.
7.15: In this meaningless life, I have seen everything, including the fact that some good people die young and some wicked people live on and on.
7.16: So don't be too good or too wise! Why destroy yourself?
7.17: On the other hand, don't be too wicked either--don't be a fool! Why should you die before your time?
7.18: So try to walk a middle course--but those who fear God will succeed either way.
7.19: A wise person is stronger than the ten leading citizens of a town!
7.20: There is not a single person in all the earth who is always good and never sins.
7.21: Don't eavesdrop on others--you may hear your servant laughing at you.
7.22: For you know how often you yourself have laughed at others.
7.23: All along I have tried my best to let wisdom guide my thoughts and actions. I said to myself, "I am determined to be wise." But it didn't really work.
7.24: Wisdom is always distant and very difficult to find.
7.25: I searched everywhere, determined to find wisdom and to understand the reason for things. I was determined to prove to myself that wickedness is stupid and that foolishness is madness.
7.26: I discovered that a seductive woman is more bitter than death. Her passion is a trap, and her soft hands will bind you. Those who please God will escape from her, but sinners will be caught in her snare.
7.27: "This is my conclusion," says the Teacher. "I came to this result after looking into the matter from every possible angle.
7.28: Just one out of every thousand men I interviewed can be said to be upright, but not one woman!
7.29: I discovered that God created people to be upright, but they have each turned to follow their own downward path."

8.1: How wonderful to be wise, to be able to analyze and interpret things. Wisdom lights up a person's face, softening its hardness.
8.2: Obey the king because you have vowed before God to do this.
8.3: Don't try to avoid doing your duty, and don't take a stand with those who plot evil. For the king will punish those who disobey him.
8.4: The king's command is backed by great power. No one can resist or question it.
8.5: Those who obey him will not be punished. Those who are wise will find a time and a way to do what is right.
8.6: Yes, there is a time and a way for everything, even as people's troubles lie heavily upon them.
8.7: Indeed, how can people avoid what they don't know is going to happen?
8.8: None of us can hold back our spirit from departing. None of us has the power to prevent the day of our death. There is no escaping that obligation, that dark battle. And in the face of death, wickedness will certainly not rescue those who practice it.
8.9: I have thought deeply about all that goes on here in the world, where people have the power to hurt each other.
8.10: I have seen wicked people buried with honor. How strange that they were the very ones who frequented the Temple and are praised in the very city where they committed their crimes!
8.11: When a crime is not punished, people feel it is safe to do wrong.
8.12: But even though a person sins a hundred times and still lives a long time, I know that those who fear God will be better off.
8.13: The wicked will never live long, good lives, for they do not fear God. Their days will never grow long like the evening shadows.
8.14: And this is not all that is meaningless in our world. In this life, good people are often treated as though they were wicked, and wicked people are often treated as though they were good. This is so meaningless!
8.15: So I recommend having fun, because there is nothing better for people to do in this world than to eat, drink, and enjoy life. That way they will experience some happiness along with all the hard work God gives them.
8.16: In my search for wisdom, I tried to observe everything that goes on all across the earth. I discovered that there is ceaseless activity, day and night.
8.17: This reminded me that no one can discover everything God has created in our world, no matter how hard they work at it. Not even the wisest people know everything, even if they say they do.

9.1: This, too, I carefully explored: Even though the actions of godly and wise people are in God's hands, no one knows whether or not God will show them favor in this life.
9.2: The same destiny ultimately awaits everyone, whether they are righteous or wicked, good or bad, ceremonially clean or unclean, religious or irreligious. Good people receive the same treatment as sinners, and people who take oaths are treated like people who don't.
9.3: It seems so tragic that one fate comes to all. That is why people are not more careful to be good. Instead, they choose their own mad course, for they have no hope. There is nothing ahead but death anyway.
9.4: There is hope only for the living. For as they say, "It is better to be a live dog than a dead lion!"
9.5: The living at least know they will die, but the dead know nothing. They have no further reward, nor are they remembered.
9.6: Whatever they did in their lifetime--loving, hating, envying--is all long gone. They no longer have a part in anything here on earth.
9.7: So go ahead. Eat your food and drink your wine with a happy heart, for God approves of this!
9.8: Wear fine clothes, with a dash of cologne!
9.9: Live happily with the woman you love through all the meaningless days of life that God has given you in this world. The wife God gives you is your reward for all your earthly toil.
9.10: Whatever you do, do well. For when you go to the grave, there will be no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom.
9.11: I have observed something else in this world of ours. The fastest runner doesn't always win the race, and the strongest warrior doesn't always win the battle. The wise are often poor, and the skillful are not necessarily wealthy. And those who are educated don't always lead successful lives. It is all decided by chance, by being at the right place at the right time.
9.12: People can never predict when hard times might come. Like fish in a net or birds in a snare, people are often caught by sudden tragedy.
9.13: Here is another bit of wisdom that has impressed me as I have watched the way our world works.
9.14: There was a small town with only a few people living in it, and a great king came with his army and besieged it.
9.15: There was a poor, wise man living there who knew how to save the town, and so it was rescued. But afterward no one thought any more about him.
9.16: Then I realized that though wisdom is better than strength, those who are wise will be despised if they are poor. What they say will not be appreciated for long.
9.17: But even so, the quiet words of a wise person are better than the shouts of a foolish king.
9.18: A wise person can overcome weapons of war, but one sinner can destroy much that is good.

10.1: Dead flies will cause even a bottle of perfume to stink! Yes, an ounce of foolishness can outweigh a pound of wisdom and honor.
10.2: The hearts of the wise lead them to do right, and the hearts of the foolish lead them to do evil.
10.3: You can identify fools just by the way they walk down the street!
10.4: If your boss is angry with you, don't quit! A quiet spirit can overcome even great mistakes.
10.5: There is another evil I have seen as I have watched the world go by. Kings and rulers make a grave mistake
10.6: if they give foolish people great authority, and if they fail to give people of proven worth their rightful place of dignity.
10.7: I have even seen servants riding like princes--and princes walking like servants.
10.8: When you dig a well, you may fall in. When you demolish an old wall, you could be bitten by a snake.
10.9: When you work in a quarry, stones might fall and crush you! When you chop wood, there is danger with each stroke of your ax! Such are the risks of life.
10.10: Since a dull ax requires great strength, sharpen the blade. That's the value of wisdom; it helps you succeed.
10.11: It does no good to charm a snake after it has bitten you.
10.12: It is pleasant to listen to wise words, but the speech of fools brings them to ruin.
10.13: Since fools base their thoughts on foolish premises, their conclusions will be wicked madness.
10.14: Foolish people claim to know all about the future and tell everyone the details! But who can really know what is going to happen?
10.15: Fools are so exhausted by a little work that they have no strength for even the simplest tasks.
10.16: Destruction is certain for the land whose king is a child and whose leaders feast in the morning.
10.17: Happy is the land whose king is a nobleman and whose leaders feast only to gain strength for their work, not to get drunk.
10.18: Laziness lets the roof leak, and soon the rafters begin to rot.
10.19: A party gives laughter, and wine gives happiness, and money gives everything!
10.20: Never make light of the king, even in your thoughts. And don't make fun of a rich man, either. A little bird may tell them what you have said.

11.1: Give generously, for your gifts will return to you later.
11.2: Divide your gifts among many, for you do not know what risks might lie ahead.
11.3: When the clouds are heavy, the rains come down. When a tree falls, whether south or north, there it lies.
11.4: If you wait for perfect conditions, you will never get anything done.
11.5: God's ways are as hard to discern as the pathways of the wind, and as mysterious as a tiny baby being formed in a mother's womb.
11.6: Be sure to stay busy and plant a variety of crops, for you never know which will grow--perhaps they all will.
11.7: Light is sweet; it's wonderful to see the sun!
11.8: When people live to be very old, let them rejoice in every day of life. But let them also remember that the dark days will be many. Everything still to come is meaningless.
11.9: Young man, it's wonderful to be young! Enjoy every minute of it. Do everything you want to do; take it all in. But remember that you must give an account to God for everything you do.
11.10: So banish grief and pain, but remember that youth, with a whole life before it, still faces the threat of meaninglessness.

12.1: Don't let the excitement of youth cause you to forget your Creator. Honor him in your youth before you grow old and no longer enjoy living.
12.2: It will be too late then to remember him, when the light of the sun and moon and stars is dim to your old eyes, and there is no silver lining left among the clouds.
12.3: Your limbs will tremble with age, and your strong legs will grow weak. Your teeth will be too few to do their work, and you will be blind, too.
12.4: And when your teeth are gone, keep your lips tightly closed when you eat! Even the chirping of birds will wake you up. But you yourself will be deaf and tuneless, with a quavering voice.
12.5: You will be afraid of heights and of falling, white-haired and withered, dragging along without any sexual desire. You will be standing at death's door. And as you near your everlasting home, the mourners will walk along the streets.
12.6: Yes, remember your Creator now while you are young, before the silver cord of life snaps and the golden bowl is broken. Don't wait until the water jar is smashed at the spring and the pulley is broken at the well.
12.7: For then the dust will return to the earth, and the spirit will return to God who gave it.
12.8: "All is meaningless," says the Teacher, "utterly meaningless."
12.9: Because the Teacher was wise, he taught the people everything he knew. He collected proverbs and classified them.
12.10: Indeed, the Teacher taught the plain truth, and he did so in an interesting way.
12.11: A wise teacher's words spur students to action and emphasize important truths. The collected sayings of the wise are like guidance from a shepherd.
12.12: But, my child, be warned: There is no end of opinions ready to be expressed. Studying them can go on forever and become very exhausting!
12.13: Here is my final conclusion: Fear God and obey his commands, for this is the duty of every person.
12.14: God will judge us for everything we do, including every secret thing, whether good or bad.

1.1: The most amazing song of all, by King Solomon.
1.2: Let him smother me with kisses—his Spirit-kiss divine. So kind are your caresses, I drink them in like the sweetest wine!
1.3: Your presence releases a fragrance so pleasing— over and over poured out. For your lovely name is “Flowing Oil.” No wonder the brides-to-be adore you.
1.4: Draw me into your heart. We will run away together into the king’s cloud-filled chamber. We will remember your love, rejoicing and delighting in you, celebrating your every kiss as better than wine. No wonder righteousness adores you!
1.5: Jerusalem maidens, in this twilight darkness I know I am so unworthy—so in need. Yet you are so lovely! I feel as dark and dry as the desert tents of the wandering nomads. Yet you are so lovely— like the fine linen tapestry hanging in the Holy Place.
1.6: Please don’t stare in scorn because of my dark and sinful ways. My angry brothers quarreled with me and appointed me guardian of their ministry vineyards, yet I’ve not tended my vineyard within.
1.7: Won’t you tell me, lover of my soul, where do you feed your flock? Where do you lead your beloved ones to rest in the heat of the day? Why should I be like a veiled woman as I wander among the flocks of your shepherds?
1.8: Listen, my radiant one— if you ever lose sight of me, just follow in my footsteps where I lead my lovers. Come with your burdens and cares. Come to the place near the sanctuary of my shepherds.
